For each entry from 0.2.0-rc.1 on, and for Unreleased once it has a line, it checks the groups and their order, three to five Highlights in a release’s entry, each collapsed group’s <details>, <summary> and blank lines, each line’s 35 words outside What to do, its details link to a releases/ page, and a full link for every issue and pull request. The entries before 0.2.0-rc.1 are history, and the test leaves them as they are.

  • The release page holds each change’s full story, and it is docs/content/docs/releases/<major>.<minor>.0.md, such as releases/0.2.0.md, which covers the release and its release candidates. Each release candidate adds its changes there, in the same commit as its changelog entry, so the page is written as the release is made. Each change gets a section of its own with its full story, under Breaking changes, Changes, Fixes and Hardening, as Writing docs describes, and the Releases section’s own page lists the page. Every fact a changelog line leaves out is in its section, so a line can stay one sentence. A change that two lines describe, such as a step in What to do and a line in Fixed, can share one section, which both link, and a line that covers several changes links each one’s section.

  • A prerelease’s changelog entry lists what changed since the version before it, whether that’s a release or another prerelease, and it becomes that prerelease’s notes on GitHub. When the release itself goes out, its entry, such as ## 0.2.0, replaces its prereleases’ entries and lists everything since the last release, so someone who upgrades from that release reads one entry. Each prerelease’s notes stay on its GitHub release.

  • Before it builds, scripts/publish.sh checks what it needs and stops with nothing done when a check fails. The tag v<version> has to pass release.sh’s own checks, so it exists, is signed, and is signed by a key in packaging/release-signer. The tag’s commit has to be main’s HEAD, and origin’s main has to be an ancestor of it, so that the push is a fast-forward. If origin already has the tag, it has to be the same tag. The working tree has to be clean, gh has to be installed and logged in (gh auth status), and minisign has to be installed. A published GitHub release for the tag is refused unless it already has every file, which is the case when an earlier run stopped after it, and unless GitHub marks it as a prerelease exactly when the version is one. The refusal names the gh release edit command that fixes the mark. The tap’s checkout, a clone of devvmhq/homebrew-tap, has to exist, be clean and be on main, for a prerelease too, and its origin has to have no commits that its main lacks. The checkout is DEVVM_TAP_DIR, or ../homebrew-tap next to this repo by default.

  • Then it builds and shows the release. It runs scripts/release.sh, which builds dist/ and signs SHA256SUMS, and where minisign asks for the password. It prints the version, the tag’s commit, each file with its size and SHA-256, the release notes, which are the CHANGELOG.md entry for the version, and the tap’s changes as a git diff of each formula it writes: Formula/devvm.rb for a release, and Formula/devvm-rc.rb, with a line saying when a release moves it too, or when it stays on a newer version. It lists the four steps, each marked done or to do, and when nothing in the tap changes, the fourth says so. Then it asks Publish devvm <version>? [y/N] on the terminal, and any answer but y stops it with nothing published. --dry-run stops before the question, so it pushes and publishes nothing and makes no commit in the tap, and --help describes the script.

  • Then it publishes, in this order. It pushes main and then the tag to origin. It makes the GitHub release devvmhq/devvm v<version> with gh release create --verify-tag, titled devvm <version>, with the release notes and the archives, the source tarball, SHA256SUMS, SHA256SUMS.minisig and install.sh. The release starts as a draft and is published only once every file is uploaded, so nobody sees a release that is missing files. Last, it copies dist/devvm.rb to the tap’s Formula/devvm.rb and dist/devvm-rc.rb to its Formula/devvm-rc.rb, each only when it’s one the tap gets and it differs, commits them in one commit, devvm <version> for a release or devvm-rc <version> for a prerelease, with the tap’s own commit signing, and pushes the tap. It uses gh for GitHub and never puts a GitHub token on a command line. At the end it prints how to check the release: brew update && brew upgrade devvm, or brew trust --formula devvmhq/tap/devvm and then brew install devvmhq/tap/devvm, with devvm-rc in place of devvm for a prerelease, and the install script’s curl line.

  • When a step fails, it says which steps it published and which it didn’t. Fix what failed and run it again, because every step skips what’s already done: a pushed main or tag, a published release whose SHA256SUMS matches the new build’s, and a tap whose formulas are already this build’s. A draft release that an earlier run left gets this build’s files again before it’s published. A release published from another build, whose SHA256SUMS doesn’t match, is refused. To finish by hand instead, run the steps it didn’t do in order: git push origin main, git push origin v<version>, the gh release create above (or gh release upload --clobber to a draft, then gh release edit v<version> --draft=false), each with --prerelease for a prerelease, and then copy the formulas the printout listed, dist/devvm.rb and dist/devvm-rc.rb, to the tap’s Formula/, commit them and push it.

  • scripts/release.sh checks the tag with git tag -v and its signer against this checkout’s packaging/release-signer, then builds dist/ from the tagged commit with GoReleaser (.goreleaser.yaml), in a clone of its own, so only what’s committed goes in, with one goreleaser release --skip=publish. It checks that the binary built for this host prints the version, writes install.sh and adds its checksum to SHA256SUMS, then signs SHA256SUMS with ~/.minisign/devvm.key (or DEVVM_MINISIGN_KEY) and verifies it with packaging/minisign.pub. Nothing is published, because publishing is scripts/publish.sh’s. scripts/release.sh --check runs only the tag’s checks and the build’s preconditions, prints the tag’s commit and builds nothing, and scripts/publish.sh runs it first.

  • dist/ then holds:

    File What
    devvm-<version>-<os>-<arch>.tar.gz the binary, its files (assets/) embedded, with README.md, CHANGELOG.md and LICENSE, for darwin and linux, arm64 and amd64
    devvm-<version>.tar.gz the source, attached to the release for whoever wants to build devvm themselves
    SHA256SUMS, SHA256SUMS.minisig their checksums and install.sh’s, and the signature
    install.sh the install script, set to this release and to packaging/minisign.pub’s key
    devvm-rc.rb the Homebrew formula devvm-rc, which follows prereleases, set to each platform’s archive, its URL and its checksum from SHA256SUMS
    devvm.rb for a release, not a prerelease, the Homebrew formula devvm, set the same way

  • scripts/release.sh --head builds from HEAD’s commit instead, for testing, with VERSION’s version, a release’s or a prerelease’s. It’s unsigned unless DEVVM_MINISIGN_KEY names a test key; DEVVM_MINISIGN_PUB names its public key in place of packaging/minisign.pub. DEVVM_RELEASE_URL points the formula at a test location. A commit without install.sh is refused.

  • scripts/release.sh --formula-from DIR writes only the formulas, for VERSION’s release once it’s published, and builds nothing: dist/devvm-rc.rb, and dist/devvm.rb too when VERSION isn’t a prerelease. Download the release’s SHA256SUMS and SHA256SUMS.minisig into DIR first. The script checks the signature against packaging/minisign.pub, and that its trusted comment is devvm <version> for VERSION’s version, so it refuses another release’s files. Then it fills in the formulas the same way a build does, from that SHA256SUMS.

  • To try dist/install.sh on such a build, copy dist/ to DIR/releases/download/v<version>/, then in a throwaway HOME with DEVVM_PREFIX under it: DEVVM_INSTALL_TEST=1 source dist/install.sh, set repo_url=file://DIR and protos='=https,file' (it downloads over HTTPS only), and run main --no-deps. Without --no-deps it offers to install what the host lacks: answer no, or run it with no terminal.

  • Every build sets the version with -X github.com/devvmhq/devvm/internal/cli.version=<version>: devvm doesn’t read VERSION. The formula template (packaging/homebrew/devvm.rb) is both formulas’ one source, and it builds nothing. It has an archive for each of macOS and Linux on arm64 and Intel, the same archives the install script installs, and it installs the binary alone from the one for this machine. release.sh fills in each formula’s class, Devvm or DevvmRc, and the other formula, which it conflicts with by its full name, devvmhq/tap/devvm-rc or devvmhq/tap/devvm, because both install the devvm command. It also fills in each archive’s URL and its checksum, which it reads from the SHA256SUMS it just wrote, on every line that isn’t a comment. Both generated formulas pass brew audit --strict --online and brew style.

  • Publishing is the maintainer’s call, so an agent asks first and never runs scripts/publish.sh without --dry-run on its own. The script’s tests (testdata/script/publish.txtar) run it against a local bare repo as origin, a local bare tap and a fake gh.

The docs sites

The docs have two sites, and the Docs workflow (.github/workflows/docs.yml) deploys both. devvm.dev shows the docs of the latest release, so what users read matches the devvm they install. next.devvm.dev shows the docs on main, for the next release, which is what someone trying a prerelease reads. A pull request that touches the docs gets their lints and a build, and it deploys nothing, so a pull request from a fork never reaches either site or its keys.

  • devvm.dev is GitHub Pages, in the repo’s github-pages environment, which accepts deployments from main and from v* tags, and only admins can create a v* tag. When a release is published, and it isn’t a prerelease, the workflow builds the docs in that release’s tag and deploys them. A release event runs the workflow file that the tag has, so a release whose tag predates this workflow doesn’t deploy on its own. Pushes to main never change devvm.dev.
  • To deploy a release’s docs by hand, for a release that didn’t deploy on its own or to put devvm.dev back on a release, run the Docs workflow from main in the repo’s Actions tab, or with gh workflow run docs.yml --repo devvmhq/devvm -f site=devvm.dev -f ref=v0.1.0. The site is devvm.dev unless you choose another one, and the ref is the release’s tag, which has to look like v0.1.0, so a prerelease’s tag is refused. Without a ref, the workflow deploys the latest release, as gh release view names it.
  • next.devvm.dev is Cloudflare Pages, serving the files on the main branch of the repo devvmhq/docs-next, and Cloudflare builds nothing. On each push to main that touches the docs, the workflow lints and builds main’s docs for next.devvm.dev, then replaces everything in devvmhq/docs-next but its README.md with the build, and commits it as Build from devvm <short sha>. When the build is the same as the last one, it commits nothing. gh workflow run docs.yml --repo devvmhq/devvm -f site=next.devvm.dev runs it by hand. Nobody edits devvmhq/docs-next by hand, because the next build replaces it.
  • Every build draws the diagrams first, with mise run docs:diagrams, so each of the workflow’s jobs installs Node through mise. A release whose tag predates the drawing script, docs/render-diagrams.mjs, loads Mermaid in its pages instead, so the release job draws them only when the tag has that script.
  • The deploy key that pushes to devvmhq/docs-next is the secret DOCS_NEXT_DEPLOY_KEY in the docs-next environment, which only main can deploy from. It’s an ed25519 key with write access to devvmhq/docs-next and to nothing else. The workflow checks that repo out with it only after the site is built, so the build never sees the key. To rotate it, make a new key, add its public half to devvmhq/docs-next as a deploy key with write access, put its private half in the secret, then delete the old deploy key.
  • The next build is hugo -s docs --minify --config hugo.yaml,next.yaml, which reads docs/next.yaml over docs/hugo.yaml. It sets the site’s address to https://next.devvm.dev/ and puts a banner on every page that says these docs are for the next devvm and links to devvm.dev. It also sets noindex, so Hextra gives every page a noindex, nofollow robots meta tag, and docs/layouts/robots.txt disallows everything, so search engines don’t index the site. devvm.dev’s build, hugo -s docs --minify, never reads docs/next.yaml, so it has no banner, its pages say index, follow, and its robots.txt allows everything.

item.title: The structure test and owners
item.description:
The structure test

internal/structure parses every Go file in the repo, tests and every platform’s included, generated files left out, and checks what linters don’t. mise run test runs it. Each failure starts with its rule and the file and line:

Rule Checks
max-methods no type has more than 24 methods, value and pointer receivers together, and no interface declares more than 24, not counting the interfaces it embeds; a larger one splits by what its methods do
no-init no func init()
package-vars a package-level var is a blank interface check, an Err*/err* sentinel from errors.New or fmt.Errorf, a regexp.MustCompile, template.Must or sync.Once* result, a //go:embed file, or listed in allowedVars; anything else becomes a field, a const or a local
layers which packages import which, in non-test files (tests may wire packages together)
owners in non-test files, only its owner runs a host command that commands lists, only the files execSites lists make a host command, only guardOwner asserts a backend package’s type, only envOwner reads a DEVVM_ variable, but the settings envSettings lists, only its file in envOwners reads HOME, only its owner’s string literals hold a text that literals lists, only its owner’s string literals are, whole, a name that names lists, only its owner’s calls to package strings split or join on a separator that separators lists, only pathsOwner builds a path in devvm’s data or config folder, and only its file in callers calls a function that callers lists (details)
goroutines in non-test files, a function that starts a goroutine, with a go statement, a wait group’s Go or time’s or context’s AfterFunc, is in goroutineSites, with what waits for its goroutines to end, or detached: and why nothing does, and a package that starts one calls leaktest.Main in its tests’ TestMain
dropped-errors in non-test files, no function assigns a Wait’s error, or a strconv parse’s, to _, such as _ = cmd.Wait() or n, _ := strconv.Atoi(s), unless droppedErrors lists it with why, because a failed wait would read as a clean exit and text that isn’t a number as 0
read-limits in non-test files, every io.ReadAll reads through an io.LimitReader made in its call, such as io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(r, limit+1)), unless unboundedReads lists its function with why, so a peer or a file that never ends can’t fill the memory
folder-ids in non-test files outside internal/platform, no function compares a folder’s identity or its volume with == or !=, except with "", switches on one, passes one to strings.EqualFold, strings.Compare, slices.Contains or slices.Index, or keys a map by one, whether indexed or in a map’s literal, with its type written out or as a named map type of the module’s. A folder’s identity is a field named Folder or GitID, a call of a state’s Folder or FolderVolume, a call of FolderID, folderID or FolderDevice, or a name in the same function that one of those, or such a name, was assigned to. A function passes when exactFolderIDs lists it with why. The rule is there because a boot can number an unchanged folder’s device anew, which only platform.SameFolder and platform.SameOpenFolder allow for
status-lines in non-test files outside the folders statusFree lists, a function that does slow work shows a status line itself, with a Reporter’s Status, a LoggedCmd step or its Runner’s Run, unless statusSites lists it with why, so the user sees what devvm waits for (status lines). Slow work is making a host command with exec.Command or exec.CommandContext, running host git through internal/hostgit, walking a folder with fs.WalkDir, filepath.Walk, filepath.WalkDir, hostsafety.Walk or safefile.Walk, looking up a volume with platform.VolumeUUID, making a request with internal/fetch’s Open, Resolve, Get or Download, waiting for a lock with platform.LockFile, LockFileShared or LockDir whose waiting is nil or platform.NoWait, or running a backend’s command outside a step with its Runner’s Output or Attach

The layers:

  • Only cmd/devvm and internal/cli import internal/ui; only internal/cli imports internal/vm; only cmd/devvm imports internal/cli.
  • internal/backend/... imports none of internal/vm, build, tools, netpolicy, secrets, project, gitprotect, sshconfig, sshagent, trust or vmssh, so the port forwarder and the link sessions stay devvm’s on every backend.
  • Only internal/backend/registry and internal/cli import a backend (lima); only tests import backendtest, internal/leaktest, internal/memnet, and internal/stubtest and the packages below it, which import only internal/msg and each other. The stubs’ binary, internal/stubtest/stub, and its state, internal/stubtest/stubstate, import nothing else of devvm’s, because the binary stands in for the tools devvm runs and is built apart from it.
  • internal/proxy imports no other devvm package except internal/daemon, internal/landlock, internal/redact, internal/safefile and internal/vmname.
  • assets, locales, internal/platform, internal/msg/gen, internal/testbuild, internal/hostgit, internal/shell, internal/vmname, internal/daemon, internal/fetch, internal/jsonc, internal/redact, internal/agents, internal/safefile, internal/landlock, internal/leaktest and internal/memnet import no devvm package; internal/agentlogin only internal/agents, internal/fetch, internal/jsonc, internal/platform, internal/proxy, internal/redact, internal/safefile and internal/state, because it holds agents’ logins; internal/msg only locales and internal/vmname; internal/paths only internal/msg and internal/vmname; internal/state only internal/msg, internal/paths, internal/platform and internal/vmname; internal/image only assets, internal/agents, internal/msg, internal/paths and internal/shell; internal/devcontainer only internal/image, internal/jsonc, internal/msg and internal/shell.

Everything it holds the code to is in devvm() in internal/structure/structure_test.go:

  • largeTypes lists the types allowed more methods, which are paths.Dirs and ui.UI, each with its count as its maximum and why. A backend isn’t one of them, because its methods are split by backend.Backend’s roles (how a backend plugs in). One that grows fails; one that shrinks fails until its maximum is lowered.
  • allowedVars lists the other package-level vars, by package folder and name, each with why: values set by -ldflags, fixed tables, test fixtures. An entry whose var is gone fails.
  • layers is the layering table: a layer’s packages (from, but not exceptFrom) import none of to (but exceptTo); x/... is x and the packages below it.
  • commands maps a host command to the one package that runs it. execSites lists the files that make a host command with exec.Command or exec.CommandContext, each with why, and a listed file that no longer makes one fails. guardOwner names internal/backend/guard.go, the one file that asserts a backend’s type. envOwner names the one file that reads devvm’s DEVVM_ variables. envSettings lists the variables read elsewhere, each with the files that read it and why. A listed file that no longer reads its variable fails. envOwners maps another variable to the one file that reads it, which for HOME is internal/paths/dirs.go.
  • literals maps a text that only one package’s string literals may hold to that package and what the others use instead. names maps a name that only one package’s string literals may be, whole, to that package and what the others use, and namesFree lists the folders whose literals may be one anyway: internal/stubtest, whose stubs are named after the commands they stand in for.
  • goroutineSites lists every function outside tests that starts a goroutine, as its file and its name (internal/proxy/splice.go: splice, or Type.Method for a method). A function literal’s goroutine counts in the function it’s in, or in the package-level var whose value it is. A goroutine starts with a go statement, a wait group’s Go, or time’s or context’s AfterFunc, whose function runs in a goroutine of its own. Goroutines that the standard library starts otherwise, such as an HTTP server’s for each connection, are for the leak checks to find, not the registry. Each entry says what waits for the goroutines to end, such as scanAll's wg.Wait, or starts with detached: and says why nothing does and what ends them anyway, such as a look at a folder whose disk may hang, which folderWithin leaves to finish on its own. A new goroutine fails until its function is listed, and a listed function that no longer starts one fails, so the list stays current. A package that starts a goroutine also fails until a test file of its calls leaktest.Main. The tests’ own goroutines are the leak checks’.
  • droppedErrors lists the functions outside tests that assign a Wait’s or a strconv parse’s error to _, each named as in goroutineSites and with why, and none does today. The check reads no types, so a call of any method named Wait counts, and the parses are Atoi, the Parse functions, Unquote, UnquoteChar and QuotedPrefix. A listed function that no longer drops one fails, so the list stays current.
  • unboundedReads lists the functions outside tests whose io.ReadAll reads with no limit, in the same way, each with why its reader ends: the status line’s look at the end of the run’s own log, which only that run writes, and the test stubs’ reads of the standard input that devvm under test writes and closes. A reader limited before the call, held in a variable, counts as unlimited, so the limit goes in the call itself. A listed function that no longer reads with no limit fails.
  • exactFolderIDs lists the functions outside tests and internal/platform that compare a field named Folder or GitID with == or !=, in the same way, each with why: the agents’ and exports’ fields of that name, which are paths, recordMove’s check that the state is as it was read, and folderChanged, which runs after a start recorded the folder’s identity as it is now. The check reads no types, so any field by those names counts. A listed function that no longer compares one fails.
  • statusSites lists the functions outside tests that do slow work and show no status line of their own, in the same way, each with why: the status line of the caller it runs under, named by its message, such as checking_vm for a launch’s checks of the project folder, work that takes the terminal, such as ssh-add asking for a passphrase, a process with no UI, such as a forwarder or a link session, or a command made for its caller to run. statusFree lists the folders whose code shows none, each with why: internal/ui, which draws the status line, the proxy’s and devvm’s background processes, internal/hostgit and internal/fetch, whose callers’ functions are the sites, and the tests’ stubs. The check reads no types, so it doesn’t see a backend’s methods, such as Exec, which TestLaunchStatusLines checks for a launch, and a caller’s status line is only named, so a reviewer checks that it covers the call. A listed function that no longer does slow work without one fails.
  • callers maps a function to the one file outside its package that calls it, and a listed file that no longer calls it fails. A method is listed as pkg.Type.Name, such as internal/paths.Dirs.AgentSettings, and any call of a method by that name outside its package counts, because the check reads no types, so a listed method’s name is its type’s alone.

TestRulesFail breaks each rule, and each layer, on small sources and checks the failure names it.

Shell scripts that live in Go strings get shellcheck too, since lint’s shellcheck only finds files with a shebang. TestEmbeddedScripts in internal/structure finds every call site that runs a script as sh -c, /bin/sh -c or bash -c (or -lc), in a []string literal or a call’s arguments, outside tests and the stubs. When the script is a constant, a literal, or a sum of them, such as seedApply with seedMarker in it, the test writes it to a file and runs shellcheck -s sh or -s bash, as its shell reads it, at -S warning, skipping when shellcheck isn’t installed. A script built at run time can’t be read there, so the test fails on one until dynamicScripts lists its file and expression with why: a fixed command around quoted paths, a devcontainer’s own command, or a builder that a test of its package checks, as internal/vm’s TestBuiltScriptsShellcheck does for the scripts built from the agents’ registry. A listed site that’s gone fails too, so the list stays current. A shell given any other flag, such as sh -ec or sh -e -c, fails as well, because the test would miss its script: put options such as set -e in the script instead. -s, for a script on standard input, is fine.

One owner for each concern

Each concern in devvm has one owner, the package or function that does it, such as internal/hostgit for every git command devvm runs on the host, internal/paths for every folder and file devvm uses, internal/settings for every default (settings.Read and settings.Save, over config.toml and settings.json, with each value’s parser), and locales/en.toml for every message. Before you add a helper, a parser, a path, a file reader, a message or a table, find its owner and extend it. A second copy drifts from the first, and then one of them is wrong. Code with no owner yet can have a second copy, because a copy can be cheaper than the wrong shared helper, so extract an owner at the third copy. A judge, such as proxy.Public or NormHost, gets its owner at once, because its two copies would disagree on what’s allowed. The packages says what each package owns, and the failures of the checks below name the owners too.

The packages

Each package owns these concerns, and a package’s doc.go, where it has one, maps the package itself. internal/fetch, internal/redact, internal/agents, internal/jsonc, internal/shell, internal/vmname, internal/safefile, internal/landlock and internal/daemon use the standard library alone, and internal/proxy uses it with internal/daemon, internal/landlock, internal/redact, internal/safefile and internal/vmname and nothing else. internal/devcontainer imports no module from outside devvm, but it uses internal/image, internal/jsonc, internal/msg and internal/shell.

Package Owns
cmd/devvm the entry point: ui.Main makes the run’s UI and runs the root command with it, and it’s the only os.Exit
internal/cli the command line. Each Cobra command has a file of its own, and its about holds its docs page, its help group and the reason it has no --json. The package also holds the run’s services (app.go), the argument and flag checks, whose failures are usage errors, help, --json, the CLI tests, docgen/, which writes the CLI reference, and doctor’s check of Linux’s pins (pins.go)
internal/vm what each command does to a folder’s VM, below the command line: Env and its parts, the one start, the finder, the inventory, Launch, the agents’ store, logins and saves, Lifecycle and the one remake, Housekeeping, Settings, Net and Links, which its doc.go maps with their owners. A --clone VM’s copy is cloneseed.go’s: its in-VM scripts initRepos, seedStage and seedApply, sent through the backend’s Exec, with the shallow file read through internal/safefile and the pack made by internal/hostgit’s git. Its uncommitted changes are cloneworktree.go’s seedTree: the index read through internal/safefile and normalised by internal/hostgit’s git, hostgit.DiffFiles for what differs, and each working copy read through a safefile.Root, opening each folder from its parent with OpenDir, so no link on the way is followed, then the record of what went, which clonecheck.go reads back. An operation in progress, the info files and the stash are clonestate.go’s seedState, each file read through internal/safefile, and only the files its stateIDs lists are read for object ids. The settings and hooks are cloneconfig.go’s seedConfig, an allowlist of config keys whose URLs cleanURL takes the credentials out of, and a VM’s stash entry is saved by clonesave.go, without its untracked files. Tools.update is the step devvm tools update takes, which devvm update takes first, and filePorts works out a VM’s ports again from its devcontainer.json’s, with the rules of devvm ports add and devvm ports rm (reading the devcontainer.json again). vm.AgentImport reads each agent’s folder through that folder as an os.Root (links out of an agent’s folder). Launch.buildTools builds the tool images that a VM’s shared tools need and the share lacks, and retainTools is retention’s tools.unused-age. Inventory.GitKeeper names the VM that keeps a path locked, and cloneState is the script that reads a --clone VM’s state back, its stash entries included. A Git LFS object file is opened beneath the common dir through an os.Root, each folder on the way checked first, because an os.Root still follows a link that stays inside it. confinementFor chooses a start’s confinement from the tier, starter.start registers the interrupt’s cleanup around the backend’s Start, vm.Env.Terminal gives an agent’s login the terminal’s files (ui.Terminal), and AgentLogin.endLogin ends the login in the VM
internal/shell quoting for a POSIX shell (Quote, QuoteJoin), a word on one line for bash (QuoteLine, ANSI-C quoting) and a shell variable’s names (EnvName), with the standard library alone
internal/vmname the name of every machine devvm runs on a backend, VM, which a field or a parameter holds instead of a string, and the parsers that make one where it’s read. Parse reads a project VM’s name from an argument or a file name, and it also reads vm.json’s name and runs in project.Nth. ParseListed reads one that a backend lists. VM’s UnmarshalText reads one in a JSON file, which may be any machine’s, so a field that must hold a project VM’s is still checked with IsProject. Image names an image’s machine, and VM.Aside a remake’s old one. msg.M.VM reads back the VM a message’s function took. It also holds a project VM’s name grammar (Prefix, HashLen, IsVM, and VM’s IsProject, Hash, Slug, Short, ImageKey and a remake’s Aside), with the standard library alone, so the proxy uses it too (the checks on owners)
internal/project a project folder: its VM’s name, the hash that names its VM’s state folder (project.Hash), its link targets, the folders that aren’t safe to use and its parents
internal/gitprotect .git protection: one scan for each check, a Locker for each host, which is Flags on macOS, Binds on Linux, whose pins the start sets, or else Watch, and the table of its reports. A nested repo is left to another only when that repo’s scan locks its git folder whole (snapshot.covered). gitprotect.Protector.Check is the check of a stopped VM, and for a VM that devvm 0.1.0 or 0.1.1-rc.1 made strict, the converter’s unstrict then takes diff.ignoreSubmodules = all out of its repos’ configs, on a context that an interrupt doesn’t cancel (context.WithoutCancel), and strictLeft does the same for devvm git-protect on and off and devvm rm, without the warning. gitprotect.Keeps says whether another VM’s protection still covers a path. The configs it reads, the watch’s hashed files and git’s .git, commondir and gitdir files all go through internal/safefile (.git protection)
internal/hostsafety the folder’s other checks on the host: one Walk once the VM is stopped, which skips .git and finds set-id files and nested repos (hostsafety.Walk, which only starter.walk calls), git’s own test for a bare repo’s shape (hostsafety.IsGitDir), doctor’s read of safe.bareRepository (hostsafety.BareExplicit), and an SSH origin
internal/hostgit every git command devvm runs on the host, with no fsmonitor, hooks, filters or signing programs, ssh only, none of the environment’s GIT_* variables and no prompts, and with GIT_NO_REPLACE_OBJECTS=1 and GIT_GRAFT_FILE=/dev/null, so it sees a repo’s real history. hostgit.UserConfig reads one key of git’s global and system config by the files’ names, the files that GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL and GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM name included
internal/sshconfig the ssh config that reaches running VMs by name, and its Include line in ~/.ssh/config
internal/sshagent each VM’s choice of SSH agent, devvm’s own agent and its keys
internal/build building and rebuilding images, and their records. build.Names checks an image name’s layers and refuses a shared tool’s name
internal/image image keys and names, with no side effects, and the shared tools’ registry, SharedTools: one entry for each toolchain, with its members, its detection, its installer, its guest environment, its PATH folders and its version files (the structure test’s names), and whether it’s built for glibc alone (image.ToolDef.GlibcOnly)
internal/fetch every HTTP client, with the standard library alone: NewClient, with a timeout and HTTPSOnly or SameScheme, Retry and Transient, ReadCapped, Get, Resolve, which finds where a HEAD’s redirects end, and Download, which checks the SHA-256 and caps the size. fetch.Client.Trust adds your CAs to a client’s roots, for the download of devvm’s own mise and an agent’s OAuth refresh
internal/upgrade devvm upgrade: how this devvm was installed (Detect), the releases (Source, with the newest, Check for a notice, and Fetch, which checks minisign’s ED signature by the built-in key, then the SHA-256), the unpack, the link’s switch and its rollback, and Homebrew. upgradetest/, for tests only, has a TLS release server and a minisign signer
internal/from --from: references, registry digests with an anonymous token, Docker’s IDs and the recorded digests
internal/redact passwords out of logs, with the standard library alone, and Secret, the type of the values that let whoever holds them act as you or as a VM (Secrets in the code). String redacts the run log’s lines, taking out proxy keys and URL passwords. In redacts another program’s log as it grows, in place and keeping its length. It reads a line not yet ended again from its start when the line is within MatchMax of what an earlier look read, and otherwise from MatchMax back, starring what runs on to an @ there, and Look.Cut does the same after a rotation’s cut. Unended redacts a copy’s cut end
internal/vmlog every log a VM can drive, except the proxy’s own. Limit is the rate and length of what a VM makes devvm’s background processes write. The port forwarder and the link session write through it, and the link session’s warnings take their turns from its Allow. Capped is a background process’s log, held to its cap as it appends, with Trim at its next start. KeepVM is what the VM’s proxy (through proxy.IO.KeepLogs) and a build run on the logs the backend writes as the VM runs (backend.Run.Logs), the serial consoles’ among them. It watches each log in a goroutine of its own, redacts what each one gained every second (redact.In), so a reboot in place can’t leave the proxy’s password there, and skips a log that hasn’t grown. Redact is Lima’s redaction at the end of a start. Each rotation copies the log’s end to its .1 file, redacting only what the last look didn’t reach and masking a secret cut at its end, and empties it with f.Truncate, counting a log by what it holds past the hole its writer left, as Lima’s programs write at their own offset. Every log is opened through safefile (Opts.Write), never through a link or waiting on a FIFO. The proxy, which imports only the standard library and a few of devvm’s leaves, rotates its own logs itself (proxy.rotating)
internal/safefile every read of a file a VM can write or swap, with the standard library alone, so the proxy uses it too (the checks on owners). It refuses a file that isn’t regular with safefile.ErrNotRegular and one past its cap with safefile.ErrTooLong
internal/landlock the proxy’s child’s confinement on Linux, with the standard library alone, behind its own build tags: Self, which confines every thread of the process to its folders with no_new_privs, Landlock and the hand-written seccomp filter (filter), checks that it holds, and returns what it got (Result), which the proxy’s confineSelf turns into its line in run/proxy.confined (proxy.Confinement) (the child’s sandbox). It makes each call on every thread through syscall.AllThreadsSyscall, which works only without cgo
internal/devcontainer a project’s devcontainer.json, with no side effects: finding it, mapping it to a new VM’s plan, its refusals, and what devvm update’s second reading replaces (Reread): devcontainer.Reread drops the parts the file gave that it no longer calls for and adds the ones it now calls for
internal/jsonc JSON with comments (jsonc.Strip), with the standard library alone
internal/tools the shared tools: the lock, mise on the host, the daily check, the tool images’ builds and the share. Share.Build builds a VM’s tool images under the making lock, which tools.Making holds, and tools.HasBuilds refuses a glibc-only tool, such as pi, for a musl VM. ShareBusy says whether another devvm holds the share’s lock, so retention skips the tool images that day. Share.NoVM lists the current tool images that no VM’s state lists, and Versions.StaleMise the folders of mise’s other versions, which gc deletes. withSDKDownloads in internal/tools/dotnet.go adds each platform’s dotnet SDK archive to the lock (building tools)
internal/netpolicy network policy: the choice of tier, learning the hosts a VM reached, RiskOf, the VM’s proxy and the self-check. netpolicy.Policies lists a VM’s policies for its tier, the built-in ones and yours, and netpolicy.PolicyWarnings warns of the lines that aren’t rules. netpolicy.Proxy.Prepare readies a VM’s proxy at each launch, its policy warnings and the CA bundle included, netpolicy.Proxy.PrepareRunning checks what could refuse a running VM’s new proxy before the old one stops, and netpolicy.Proxy.Refusal runs the company proxy’s check with the check of your CAs. The event log’s readers are netpolicy.Log.Blocks, which gives a quiet block no Allow, netpolicy.Log.Learned, with Learned.NoProxy for the hosts that only transparent mode reached and agentWord for a User-Agent’s first word, Log.Countable and netpolicy.Log.MarkLearning. netpolicy.Judge.Quiet keeps quiet hosts out of what devvm network lock offers, netpolicy.Tickable, with its list tickable, and netpolicy.RiskOf mark the hosts it offers, and quietMark and RuleFile.Quiet show the quiet lines in devvm network (network policy)
internal/secrets tokens on the host and the VM’s bindings to them, and your own secrets (custom.go, with their checks, Yours and custom-secrets.json). secrets.BoundSecret records in a VM’s state the definition and hosts a secret of yours was bound with, and the store’s lookup (Store.Get, secrets.Store.Get) checks every binding against that record. secrets.Store.Save saves a secret, secrets.ClaudeOf(store).Login picks the one Claude Code login devvm keeps, and secrets.ClaudeOf(store).Sums gives that login’s checksums
internal/trust your CAs in ~/.config/devvm/ca, read and checked, sent to VMs, the build VMs’ Trust scripts and the guest environment, and each VM’s own CA and its next one (InitCA, in vms/<hash>/run/ca/). trust.Env holds the CAs’ variables that a build’s scripts and every project VM start with. trust.Read reads your CA folder, looking at each file with os.Lstat and following no link, trust.CAs.Host writes the bundle for the host’s mise on Linux, and trust.InitCA readies each VM’s CA and its next one
internal/agents the coding agents’ registry, with the standard library alone: one Def for each agent, with its shared tool, settings, logins, history, guest environment, ways to log in and [pass-keys], which every list of the agents comes from. Code about one agent names it by its constant (the structure test’s names). agents.Def’s PassKeys says whether an agent’s keys are withheld by default, and agents.Providers lists the providers whose keys the proxy puts in
internal/agentlogin agents’ login and settings files on the host: the VM’s copies with placeholders, the bindings, the values and the OAuth refresh (File, with a format for each kind of login), the shape of every placeholder (Placeholder), Redact, and Restore, which puts the store’s values back for a VM’s placeholders. The package agentlogin saves a captured login (agentlogin.File.Capture), refreshes and reads one (agentlogin.File.Get) and makes the VM’s copy (agentlogin.File.VMCopy), whose VMFile reports PassBound, the bound providers that [pass-keys] lists. agentlogin.Pick tells whose login a request is by its User-Agent, agentlogin.Endpoints lists every format’s endpoints, agentlogin.SetupToken recognises claude setup-token’s request, agentlogin.ClaudeOAuthBindings makes the Claude login’s bindings, agentlogin.OpencodeImport makes opencode’s import entries, and agentlogin.PiSettings drops the pi settings that would undo devvm’s. The formats’ field lists are codexKeep, claudeAccountKeep and cursorFormat, internal/agentlogin/logins.go holds opencodeVM and withheldEntry, and internal/agentlogin/pi.go holds pi’s format (agents’ logins and settings)
internal/proxy the proxy, as its README.md describes. It runs as two processes, its broker, devvm _proxy (broker.go, process.go), and its child, devvm _proxy-child (child.go), which talk over a socketpair in the broker’s protocol (wire.go). The package also holds the relay of a VM’s SSH agent on paths.Dirs.AgentRelay (Config.Agent, agent.go), which is the only socket of an agent that a VM’s backend forwards. And it holds the one form of a host that every package judges and compares hosts in (Host, NormHost, HostOK), which the structure test holds every package to (the checks on owners). The desktop’s local proxy listens in the VM at proxy.LocalProxyAddr and proxy.LocalProxyPort (the local proxy). The package proxy reads policies in policy.go: proxy.ParsePolicy is the one parser of every policy file, which returns each line with its number and whether it’s a rule, proxy.ValidRule decides what’s a rule, proxy.BrokenDeny marks a broken ! line, and proxy.ReadPolicy reads a file through internal/safefile. readBuiltins keeps a built-in policy’s quiet lines (PolicyLine.Quiet), and loadPolicy drops any other file’s. proxy.NarrowRule writes a rule by method and path in its canonical form, in proxy.Methods’ order, and proxy.ExactRule the exact rule for one host and port. proxy.ReadAllowlist reads the allowlist tier’s policies, whose Allowlist.Allows, Allowlist.Denies and Allowlist.Quiet are the proxy’s own decisions. A decision reads the rules that cover a host and port in one read (policy.rulesFor, a hostRules), policy.all leaves the quiet rules out and policy.quiet matches them. hostRules.byRequest says when requests are judged one by one, by policy.judge, and hostRules.unjudgeable covers a request that names a method outside proxy.Methods. request.go judges each request in an intercepted tunnel (server.judgeRequest) with the one matcher of rules and bindings, proxy.match, which uses plainPath, proxy.PathOK and matchPath for paths and patterns, overrides and overrideLike for the methods a request names, and match.allows, match.denies and trimDots, and Go’s url.ParseQuery, whose ParseQuery reads a query differently from some servers (requests by method and path). In proxy.go, server.blocked marks a block’s event Quiet only for the reason notAllowed, blockPage writes the block page, and proxy.Public is the one judge of a public address. secrets.go holds the bindings file (proxy.BindingList.Encode), how a secret binding’s value goes in (Binding.secretValue) and a login binding’s (Binding.takes), and the refusals githubMinting and cursorMints. cursor.go holds Cursor’s routes and refusals (cursorRoutes, cursorPersists, cursorStore, cursorChanges) and the reply scanners (frameScanner, jwtScanner). upstream.go holds the route to a company proxy (proxy.Upstream.WithPassword, proxy.Upstream.Route), which a lookup’s context carries with proxy.WithRoute and gives back with proxy.RouteOf, and the CAs a lookup trusts (proxy.WithRoots, proxy.RootsOf). The config is proxy.Config, and proxy.Config.Sum tells devvm whether a running proxy must start again
internal/seatbelt macOS’s sandbox as devvm uses it: sandbox-exec’s path (Exec), a Seatbelt string and a real path in a profile (String, Path), the links a sandboxed lookup goes through (Links), and the profile of a VM’s proxy’s child (ChildProfile), which Sandbox.ProxyChild gives the broker through proxy.IO.Seatbelt, because the proxy imports the standard library alone. Lima’s profile for its hostagent (lima/seatbelt.go) is written with the same strings and paths. How the child is confined, its report in run/proxy.confined (proxy.Confinement), the check that it holds (checkConfined) and the hook where a platform confines the child in the process (confineSelf) are internal/proxy’s confine.go, which every platform’s confinement shares
internal/daemon devvm’s background processes, with the standard library alone: detached starts in a session of their own (daemon.Detach), pid files checked against the process’s arguments before any signal (daemon.Proc), stopping with TERM and then KILL, each sent to the process’s group (daemon.SignalGroup), readiness by a status file, the lifeline, and an accept loop’s wait after an error that leaves its listener open (AcceptRetry), which the port forwarder, the link session, a login’s forward, the proxy’s SSH agent relay and the desktop relay share. It’s the only place that signals a process by its pid. Processes has what each of those processes holds, reads, writes and is confined by
internal/desktop devvm desktop’s relay on the host, which checks VNC’s password, then opens an ssh channel to the VM’s socket and drops the viewer’s clipboard, and the desktop’s passwords
internal/backend Backend and its roles, Caps, Require, Check, the registry and its guard (As), as how a backend plugs in describes. Below it are backendtest/, the fake, registry/, which holds every backend, and lima/, whose pins.go has QEMU’s user and mount namespace on Linux, its pins, their events and the probe, while platform’s pinrun_linux.go is the namespace’s side. A build’s ImageSpec.Trust, a Trust, holds the Add and Remove scripts made from ca.sh and the Env each script gets, and a tools build runs ToolsSpec.Trust.Add alone. A backend runs Add before anything downloads and Remove once the scripts are done: Lima runs Add right after the start and Remove before the final sync, and a tools build needs no Remove. backend.NetProxy confines a VM to its proxy and backend.NetDirect puts it on its backend’s own network, Confinement.GuestProxy says whether the guest’s proxy settings name devvm’s proxy, and Lima’s clone sets the VM’s environment from VMSpec.Env (a company’s CA in builds)
internal/vmssh devvm’s own use of a VM’s ssh, on every backend. Checked is the one way to a VM’s ssh (how a backend plugs in), and Forwards is the port forwarder’s one owner, which locks, stops and starts it with its ports from vm.json. The package also holds a login’s forward of this machine’s loopback ports, in devvm’s own process (ForwardLoopback), the links’ sessions, and each VM’s one record of its host keys for each start (PinHostKeys, in vms/<hash>/run/known_hosts), which every ssh of devvm’s checks
internal/ui the only package that prints: ui.UI, with messages, prompts, the status line, the run log and the cleanups, and ui.Main, which handles signals. It has no package state
internal/msg, locales messages: en.toml, the generated functions, the doc links (docs.go), the generator (gen/), Reporter and Question (messages)
internal/ports a VM’s ports section, with the forwards asked for and the host ports chosen, and the one allocator of host ports, under the claims lock, which puts VMs’ ssh only on the ports browsers refuse (SSHPorts)
internal/paths every folder and file devvm uses, a VM’s in its folder (Dirs.VM, and a project VM’s folder, vms/<hash>/, from Dirs.VMDir), and host paths resolved and compared (Physical, PhysicalParent, Within, Below, In and Under, where resolve.go says which one is for what). Among the locks, paths.Dirs.GitLock is the host’s lock of .git protection, taken before any VM’s own, and Dirs.MakingLock is the tool images’ making lock
internal/state a VM’s state, vm.json, with its core fields and one section for each package, which changes only in VM.Update under the VM’s lock. It also owns the layout version (CheckLayout and migrations, while testdata/script/layout.txtar lists every file), every file written whole (WriteFile, WriteFileMode) and private folders (PrivateDir)
internal/settings the defaults (Defaults, Read, Save), with your config.toml, read strictly, over devvm’s settings.json, and each value’s check (ParsePorts, ParseCPUs, ParseGiB and the retention settings). settings.CompanyProxy.Upstream checks the company proxy’s settings and its password, settings.CompanyProxy.Route is the route devvm’s own clients take through it, and settings.PassKeys is config.toml’s [pass-keys]
internal/platform the code for each system, behind build tags, such as platform.SameFolder, which tells whether a project folder whose device number changed after a restart is still the VM’s (an existing VM), and platform.FoldsCase, whether the system’s file systems fold case
internal/ubuntu finding Ubuntu’s cloud image and verifying it, without ever downloading one, the release pocket’s date (ubuntu.Released), and versions ordered as dpkg --compare-versions orders them (ubuntu.CompareVersions)
internal/testbuild whether this is a test build, which ldflags set: only a test build reads the test overrides (cli’s readOverrides)
assets the files devvm ships, embedded as assets.FS, which cli passes to constructors. base.yaml is base’s Lima template, and prelude.sh, with $devvm_arch, $devvm_libc and devvm_sha, comes first in each build script run with bash, the user’s layers included, and is put in place of a script’s #! line, as one eval line quoted by shell.QuoteLine, by image.WithPrelude, which image.OwnScript calls for devvm’s own. layers/ holds base’s scripts, its policy and Ubuntu’s signing keys, and the built-in layers, desktop, docker and nix, each with its policy. network/ holds the network tiers’ own policies, features/ base’s optional features, and shared-tools/ its mise.toml, build.sh and *.policy files. guest/ holds the scripts in the VM that every launch sends, and the port forwarder’s ports.sh, and oci/ is --from’s conversion, as its README.md describes. So the How it works pages’ scripts are, in the repo, assets/base.yaml, assets/prelude.sh, assets/layers/apt.sh, whose first step is assets/layers/apt.sh begin, assets/layers/base.sh, assets/layers/<name>.sh for each built-in layer, which are assets/layers/desktop.sh, assets/layers/docker.sh and assets/layers/nix.sh, with assets/layers/desktop.policy, assets/layers/docker.policy and assets/layers/nix.policy, Ubuntu’s keys, assets/layers/ubuntu-cloud.gpg and assets/layers/ubuntu-archive.gpg, base’s features, assets/features/<name>.sh, the shared tools’ assets/shared-tools/mise.toml and assets/shared-tools/build.sh, the conversion’s assets/oci/build.sh and assets/oci/bootify.sh, and the CA script, assets/guest/ca.sh, which assets/guest/ca.sh DIR runs to install the CAs in a VM. The built-in policies are paths in assets/ (images)
internal/structure the structure test, for tests only, and owners_doc_test.go, which writes the checks on owners
internal/stubtest the test stubs, for tests only
internal/leaktest the goroutine leak checks, Main for a package’s TestMain and Check for one test, for tests only, and the standard library only, so the proxy’s tests use it too
internal/memnet the network in memory for tests in a synctest bubble: connections (Pipe) that close their writing side alone, hold a buffer’s worth and have deadlines, and listeners by address (Network), for tests only, and the standard library only, so the proxy’s tests use it too
testdata the CLI tests (script/*.txtar), the golden fixtures (golden/<os>/), a lock to test with (mise.lock), each package’s coverage baseline on each system (coverage/<os>.txt), each release’s state fixture (v<release>/<os>/), and the lines that break each forbidigo rule (lint/, Go lint rules)
tests/e2e, tests/e2e-mise.lock the end-to-end tests on real VMs, in Go with the tag e2e and a file for each section. TestE2E is the run, sandbox_test.go has the sandbox, its slot’s paths and lock and e2eUbuntuRelease, and slots_test.go runs the slots. The lock file holds the shared tools’ versions that every section but tools uses (scripts/bump.sh e2e-tools)
scripts, packaging, .goreleaser.yaml, VERSION, CHANGELOG.md bump.sh updates the pins. release.sh runs the signed tag’s checks around GoReleaser, then minisign, and publish.sh makes the release itself, with its checks, release.sh, one yes, then the pushes, gh release and the tap. The test and coverage tasks run test.sh, which runs coverage.sh to check each package’s coverage against its baseline. packaging/ holds the Homebrew formula and key.go, which embeds its folder, so devvm upgrade’s key is minisign.pub’s, and a build without that file has none. Only the scripts read VERSION (releasing)
install.sh curl | bash: it installs the host’s archive, with the binary, the README, the changelog and the license, checked, into ~/.local/lib/devvm/<version>, then runs doctor’s fixes, asking first. Tests source it (DEVVM_INSTALL_TEST)

The checks on owners

An owner gets a check only when a second copy would be a bug or a security hole, and only when the check is exact, so that it never fails on code that’s right. Each check’s failure names the owner. The table is written from ownerDocs in internal/structure/owners_doc_test.go, which TestOwnersDoc checks it against and TestOwnersAgree checks against the structure test’s own tables, so a change to a check changes its row there, and go test ./internal/structure -run TestOwnersDoc -update writes the table again:

Check Owner Allowed elsewhere
forbidigo, testbuild.On internal/cli, whose readOverrides is the only code that asks whether this is a test build nowhere: other packages take the overrides as fields
forbidigo, os.FindProcess, syscall.Kill, unix.Kill and os.Process’s Kill and Signal internal/daemon, which signals a background process only while its pid file and its arguments say it’s still that process (Proc), or through the process it started (Handle) internal/platform; tests, which signal the children they started; and a child that hasn’t been waited for yet, whose pid is still its own, with a nolint saying so
forbidigo, unicode.IsGraphic, IsPrint, IsControl and Bidi_Control msg.Safe in internal/msg/safe.go, the one rule for which characters reach the terminal, which msg.Printable, msg.OneLine, the UI’s renderers and devvm agent save’s diff follow, so a second rule can’t let through what this one refuses (Colors says what it refuses) a check that isn’t about the terminal, such as a path one line long, with a //nolint:forbidigo saying so
forbidigo, HTTP clients internal/fetch, whose NewClient sets each client’s timeout and redirect policy (HTTPSOnly or SameScheme), and whose Retry, Transient, ReadCapped, Get, Resolve and Download try again after the failures that may pass, cap what a body or a download may hold, follow a HEAD’s redirects to where they end and check a download’s SHA-256 before anything uses it. fetch.Client is its own type, so a client that NewClient didn’t make, such as &fetch.Client{}, fails every request, and a caller changes a client’s transport through its Transport method internal/proxy, which is the standard library only, and tests, which make their own servers’ clients
forbidigo, netip.Addr’s IsPrivate proxy.Public in internal/proxy/proxy.go, the one judge of whether an address is on the internet: netip’s classes, the table of the other ranges that aren’t (notPublic), and the IPv4 address in a NAT64 or 6to4 address. The proxy’s floor, devvm network lock, a --clone VM’s partial-clone remotes and --from’s registries all ask it, so a range added to it holds for each internal/proxy
forbidigo, redact.Secret’s Reveal; the structure test, a struct that embeds redact.Secret and an interface that declares Reveal() string redact.Secret in internal/redact/secret.go, the type of the values that let whoever holds them act as the user or a VM, but for those Secrets in the code names: a VM’s proxy password, a secret’s value, a login’s keys and tokens once they leave its file, and the company proxy’s password and its Proxy-Authorization. Every way of printing one shows <redacted> or, in an unexported field, an address, and encoding one as JSON or text is an error, never a stand-in, so a file that holds the real value writes it through its own wire type, and a value can’t be lost by going somewhere it isn’t meant to where the value is used, each call to Reveal with a //nolint:forbidigo that says why: the proxy’s password check, its config file, the headers it puts values in, the company proxy’s credentials, the VM’s CA key as it signs and the broker’s frames to its child; the store’s file and Keychain; the VM’s proxy URL and its key in vm.json; a login’s file, its refresh and its claims; and tests. No struct embeds redact.Secret and no interface declares Reveal() string outside internal/redact
forbidigo, os.WriteFile, os.Create and os.O_TRUNC internal/state, whose WriteFile and WriteFileMode write a file whole through a temporary file in its folder, renamed over it, so a reader never sees half of it internal/proxy, which imports only the standard library and has its own writer, writeAtomic; internal/msg/gen, which imports no devvm package; internal/stubtest; tests; and, with a nolint saying why, a file written another way: a log that a process writes as it runs, a download that streams into its file, and internal/daemon’s pid and status files, each written in one write that a reader takes as missing until its line ends
forbidigo, os.Open, os.OpenFile, os.ReadFile, os.OpenRoot, os.OpenInRoot, os.DirFS and os.Root’s Open, OpenFile, ReadFile and FS, in the code that reads files a VM can write or swap: internal/gitprotect, internal/agentlogin, internal/vm’s devcontainer.go, detect.go, paste.go and agentsave*.go, internal/netpolicy/rules.go, internal/vmlog, and internal/proxy’s config.go, policy.go, rotate.go and nixcache.go internal/safefile, which imports only the standard library, so the proxy reads with it too. Its Read and Open open a file without blocking and, unless the caller passes Follow, without following a symbolic link at the path’s end. They then check the file they opened, not its name, so a FIFO, a device or a folder is refused with ErrNotRegular, a file past its cap with ErrTooLong, and, with OneLink, a file with another hard link with ErrLinked. A FIFO that the VM swaps in after a check can’t hold devvm, and a link to /dev/zero can’t flood it. Checked checks a file its caller opened another way in the same way, such as devvm paste’s copied file, which platform.OpenNoLinks opens following no link but the system’s, through openat, which the standard library doesn’t have on macOS. OpenRoot opens beneath a folder through os.Root, never through a link out of it, and its FS lists and stats what’s there but opens only regular files and, never through a link at the name’s end, folders to list. Walk walks a folder that a VM can fill, reading each folder in batches and stopping at its bound on the entries it reads, as devvm agent import walks an agent’s folder every other file, which is devvm’s own or the user’s; tests, which make their own fixtures; and, with a nolint saying why, what opens a file to write it or a folder to lock it, such as the proxy’s logs and the Nix cache’s lock, each opened never through a link or waiting on a FIFO and checked once open
forbidigo, os.Chmod, os.Chtimes, os.Chown, os.Lchown and os.Truncate, in the code that changes files a VM can write or swap: internal/proxy, internal/vmlog and internal/vmssh the file’s own descriptor, from internal/safefile, an os.Root or the proxy’s OpenLog: os.File’s Chmod, Chown and Truncate, an os.Root’s methods, and the proxy’s touchFile (futimes, or utimensat with no path), because a VM can swap a name for a link between the open and the change, which would then reach a file of yours every other package, whose files are devvm’s own or the user’s; tests, which make their own fixtures; and, with a nolint saying why, a unix socket devvm has just made in its own folder (the proxy’s SSH agent relay and the link session’s sockets), whose mode only its path can set
forbidigo, os.Setenv, os.Unsetenv, os.Clearenv and syscall’s each command’s own environment, its exec.Cmd’s Env, because every command and background process devvm starts inherits devvm’s. A VM’s SSH agent is one: the finder’s target carries its socket, its proxy’s relay (netpolicy.Proxy.Prepare), which goes to the backend in backend.ExecOpts.Agent, backend.ShellOpts.Agent and Confinement.AgentSocket, and Lima sets SSH_AUTH_SOCK on that VM’s limactl commands alone, so a run that reaches several VMs never gives one another’s daemon.Ready in internal/daemon/status.go, which takes the status file’s name out of a background process’s own environment; stubtest.NoGitRepo, which takes git’s variables that pick a repo out of a test’s environment until the test ends; and tests, which use t.Setenv
the structure test’s owners, host commands the runners: the UI’s LoggedCmd, which a package takes as a field and which runs a command into the run log, a backend’s Runner, and internal/hostgit. A host command that one of them doesn’t run is made only in the files execSites lists: those that make the command a runner then runs, such as Lima’s limactl and mise’s, and those whose command can’t go into the run log, because it streams for as long as a link, the port forwarder or the desktop’s relay lasts, asks on the terminal, outlives the run, or carries a secret tests
the structure test’s owners, a backend’s other interfaces backend.As in internal/backend/guard.go, because the registry’s backends are behind its guard, whose type has only backend.Backend’s methods, so a type assertion to backend.Forgetter or *lima.Lima on one is always false tests
the structure test’s owners, git internal/hostgit, which runs git without the repo’s fsmonitor, hooks, filters or signing programs, over ssh only, without the environment’s GIT_* variables, prompts, replace refs or grafts. It’s also the only package whose string literals may be "push", whole (names), and none is: a --clone VM’s copy goes through the backend’s Exec (internal/vm/cloneseed.go), never git’s transport, whose receive-pack refuses shallow and SHA-256 repos. Nor may any other package’s be "diff-files", which enters each submodule, where that repo’s own config can name a filter: hostgit.DiffFiles doesn’t. In tests, which run plain git to make their repos, it’s internal/stubtest’s Git, which leaves out git’s variables that pick a repo, its files or its config (GitEnv), so a git that runs the tests, such as a hook’s or git rebase --exec’s, never sends a test’s git to the checkout itself nothing else
forbidigo, os.UserHomeDir, and the structure test’s owners, HOME paths.FromEnv in internal/paths/dirs.go, which reads HOME once into paths.Dirs.Home, so a test or an e2e run that sets its own HOME moves every path devvm takes from it tests
the structure test’s owners, DEVVM_ variables readOverrides in internal/cli/overrides.go, which reads a test build’s stand-ins, while a release reads none the settings in envSettings, and tests
the structure test’s owners, shell quoting internal/shell, whose Quote and QuoteJoin quote words for a POSIX shell, so a value never runs as a command, and QuoteLine a word on one line for bash tests
the structure test’s owners, the VM-name grammar internal/vmname, whose IsVM tells a project VM’s name from an image’s, so gc never takes a project VM for an image tests
the structure test’s owners, VM names internal/vmname, whose VM is the name of every machine devvm runs on a backend: a project VM, an image’s machine, a build VM, or a VM’s old machine while a remake makes the new one. A name is made a VM only where it’s read: Parse takes a project VM’s name from an argument or a file name, and also reads vm.json’s name and runs in project.Nth, ParseListed one a backend lists, VM.UnmarshalText one in a JSON file (one path element that doesn’t start with -, or none, and any machine’s, so a field that must hold a project VM’s is still checked with IsProject), Image names an image’s machine and VM.Aside a remake’s old one, and a backend’s build VMs are typed constants. A struct field, a parameter or a result named for a VM (vm, vms, otherVM, vmName) whose type is a string, a pointer to one, a list of them or a map keyed on them fails, and so do a conversion of anything but a literal to vmname.VM and a type alias of it, so a path, an alias or a folder’s name is never passed for a VM’s name. The check goes by names, so it doesn’t see a VM’s name in a string named otherwise (target, client, parent, to, name), vmname imported with a dot or reached through a type parameter, or a VM joined to a string constant, whose type is still vmname.VM (l.VM+lineNoLinks in internal/vmssh/links.go) msg.M.VM in internal/msg/msg.go, which reads back the VM a message’s function took; internal/stubtest, whose stubs stand in for limactl and ssh, whose arguments are strings; the names notNames lists that aren’t a VM’s, such as backend.Registry.NewVMs, a backend’s name; and tests
the structure test’s owners, hosts internal/proxy/host.go, whose NormHost reads a host as the proxy judges it, the one form every judge of a host compares: a host of printable ASCII lowercased, in ASCII alone, and its one trailing dot dropped unless it’s an address, whose dot can only be its IPv6 zone’s, and any other host left as it is, which HostOK refuses, so no Unicode fold makes another name match. An address is bare, or an IPv6 address in one pair of brackets, never one with a stray bracket. Its Host is what a matcher takes, such as a rule’s matchHost and NO_PROXY’s. A call to package strings that drops a dot (Trim, TrimLeft or TrimRight with a cutset that holds ., TrimSuffix or CutSuffix with "."), or that folds or trims an argument named for a host (ToLower, ToUpper, EqualFold, TrimFunc, TrimLeftFunc or TrimRightFunc of host, sni or u.Hostname()), fails, and so does a conversion to proxy.Host of anything but a literal. The check goes by names and calls, so it doesn’t see a host’s case folded in a variable named otherwise, a dot dropped by slicing, or a host mapped rune by rune (strings.Map) the functions free lists by file and name, each with why: trimDots in internal/proxy/request.go, which drops a path’s segments’ trailing dots; urlHost in internal/vm/cloneseed.go, which reads a remote’s ssh host as ssh does, to find a VM’s alias, its case folded and its trailing dot kept; safeIndexPath in internal/vm/cloneworktree.go, which drops a path segment’s trailing dots and spaces as Windows does; and machines.fillPassword in internal/backend/lima/start.go and transportHelper in internal/vm/cloneconfig.go, which check that a string has only the characters of a set that holds .; and tests
the structure test’s owners, the coding agents internal/agents, whose Defs hold every fact devvm keeps of each agent, so no copy of an agent’s list or paths goes stale when one is added. A string literal that is an agent’s name or a login file’s kind, whole, or that holds an agent’s folder below the home folder, fails, and code of one agent’s own names the agent by its constant there. Comparing with that constant, or with one named after it such as secrets.ClaudeToken, a case for it, looking for it with slices.Contains or slices.Index, looking it up in a map, a map literal keyed on it and strings.HasPrefix, HasSuffix, EqualFold or Contains with it fail too, outside the files named for the agent, such as claude.go, so the rest of devvm asks the agent’s Def and a new agent changes none of it. A list that holds every agent’s name, tests included, fails as a copy of agents.Names(), and so does a CLI test script’s line that lists agents as a message does, for which the runner gives $AGENT_CHOICES, $LOGIN_AGENTS and $KEY_AGENTS (adding a coding agent) internal/stubtest, whose stubs are named after the commands they stand in for, and tests; for a name, the value of a constant that devvmNameFree lists with its reason and the only files that may use it: vm.CursorCommand, the Cursor editor’s cursor command, which devvm cursor runs and isn’t the agent’s, used in internal/vm/ssh.go and internal/cli/cursor.go alone and compared with as an agent’s constant is; for the comparisons, the files whose names hold the agent’s name as a word, and the constants devvmSwitchFree lists in one file each with its reason: the claude secret’s own checks, which are a secret’s, and Codex’s binding name in logins.go
the structure test’s owners, the toolchains internal/image, whose SharedTools holds every fact devvm keeps of each toolchain: its members, the files that call for it, its installer, its guest environment, its PATH folders and its version files. A string literal that is a toolchain’s name or a member’s, whole, fails, so code elsewhere asks the table, and a new toolchain is an entry there (adding a toolchain) internal/stubtest, and tests
the structure test’s owners, image names internal/image, whose Name is an image’s name and splits it into its layers (Layers, Parent, Has), whose NameOf joins layers into one, and whose ParseName reads the name the user gives, which build.Names’ Parse checks against the layers there are. devvm build, devvm rebuild and devvm images rm read their names there once, and the rest of devvm passes the image.Name on tests
the structure test’s owners, state.ReadHash and project.Parents the finder in internal/vm/finder.go, whose target finds the VM every command acts on: the folder’s own, the nearest parent folder’s under --here and --parent (resolveFolder), or one named (devvm rm VM). It finds a folder’s VM by the state that records the folder (finder.state, by the path’s hash first, then recorded), offers to move a VM whose folder moved there (moveHere in internal/vm/move.go, the match here.movedFrom), and names a new VM by the first of the folder’s names whose VM folder is free (newName, project.Nth). Its need says what the command needs of the VM, and need.check is the one place that refuses one that isn’t there, one made for an earlier folder at its path, one whose remake didn’t finish and one whose creation didn’t, the last with refuseUnfinished, which every start (starter.bringUp in internal/vm/start.go) makes too. It reads the folder devvm runs in only then, so the commands that act on no folder’s VM run in a folder that’s gone. The VM it finds is a target (internal/vm/target.go). It holds what the VM’s backend told the finder, which each start and stop of the VM then updates, and it runs what a command does with that VM: exec, shell, stop, running, ownSSH and the name of its ssh config entry internal/state, and tests
the structure test’s owners, hostsafety.Walk the start in internal/vm/start.go, whose starter.walk walks a VM’s project folder once for each check of the folder on the host, for the git repos nested in it, which .git protection goes by (gitprotect.Protector.Nested), and on Linux hosts its set-id files, so a check never walks the folder twice. It walks when a VM is made and when a check finds it stopped, at a launch or at devvm stop (starter.hostChecks), and at devvm git-protect on a stopped VM, never at a launch into a running VM internal/hostsafety, and tests
the structure test’s owners, state.ReadAll the inventory in internal/vm/inventory.go, which reads every VM’s state (ReadStates), and with ReadInventory the backends’ lists too, each within its wait, for every listing of VMs: devvm ls, devvm space, devvm images and devvm gc, the ssh config, devvm gc --orphans, the links, devvm secret’s list, finding a VM by its name and the mounts that devvm’s SSH agent checks a key against. Its one failure policy is that a backend that can’t list fails a listing (Inventory.Err) only when some VM’s state names it, and that a state that can’t be read is a row of its own, which the readers leave out and ToolsInUse and Mounts fail on. state.VMNames, which fails on such a state, stays for the readers below internal/vm that must count every VM: netpolicy’s secrets, ports and sshconfig.ChooseAlias; state.ReadableVMs, which leaves such a state out, is for those that only warn: netpolicy’s warnings of every VM and doctor’s policy warnings internal/state, and tests
the structure test’s owners, paths.Dirs.AgentSettings and paths.Dirs.AgentLogins devvm’s agent store: agentStore in internal/vm/agents.go for the agents’ settings, which the mounts, the setup’s copies, a remake’s home and devvm agent import take, and secrets.LoginFile in internal/secrets/secrets.go for their logins, which the setup’s copies and the proxy read, so nothing reads an agent’s files from the home folder but vm.AgentImport internal/paths, and tests
the structure test’s owners, paths in devvm’s folders internal/paths, whose Dirs and VM name every file and folder devvm keeps, so the layout, its golden listing in testdata/script/layout.txtar and a VM’s teardown miss none. A filepath.Join onto a Data or Config field fails, and so does an os.MkdirTemp or os.CreateTemp there whose name is a literal; a name from paths, such as paths.ToolsBuildPrefix, passes tests

forbidigo matches only the function a call names, so the checks that look at a call’s arguments are in the structure test. It finds a host command in an exec.Command or exec.CommandContext call that names it, as a literal or as a constant, whatever name the file imports os/exec under. It finds a DEVVM_ variable in a call to any function or field named Getenv or LookupEnv, in any case, so t.Getenv and a getenv parameter count as well as os.Getenv, and it finds HOME the same way. The settings envSettings lists are the ones users set, DEVVM_NO_TOOL_CHECK, DEVVM_NO_RELEASE_CHECK, DEVVM_LIMA_HOME, DEVVM_SECRET_SERVICE and DEVVM_FROM; names mode, DEVVM_MESSAGES, which any build has; and the variables devvm sets for its own processes, DEVVM_GUESTFWD for devvm _qemu and DEVVM_DAEMON_STATUS for each background process internal/daemon starts.

The structure test also finds a copy of an owner’s code by its text, in literals. A string literal outside tests that holds '\'', the escaped quote a shell quoter writes, belongs in internal/shell, and one that holds [0-9a-f]{14}, the hash at the end of a project VM’s name, belongs in internal/vmname. A quote written as a rune, such as '\'' in Go, isn’t a string literal, so it doesn’t count. One that holds a coding agent’s folder below the home folder, such as .codex/ or .pi/agent, belongs in internal/agents, and so does one that is an agent’s name or a login file’s kind, whole, such as "opencode" (names), so code of one agent’s own names it by its constant there, such as agents.Opencode, and a longer text that mentions an agent, such as a command’s example, doesn’t count. A literal that is a toolchain’s name or one of its members’, whole, such as "dotnet" or "pnpm", belongs in internal/image in the same way, so code elsewhere finds a toolchain’s facts in its image.SharedTools entry. A literal that is "push", whole, belongs only in internal/hostgit, which holds none, so no package passes push to git: a --clone VM’s copy goes through the backend’s Exec instead (internal/vm/cloneseed.go, the copy into a clone VM), because git’s receive-pack refuses shallow and SHA-256 repos, and a second transport would drift. A literal that is "diff-files", whole, belongs only in internal/hostgit too, whose DiffFiles adds --ignore-submodules=all, because git diff-files otherwise runs git status in each submodule or embedded repo, where that repo’s own config can name a filter that devvm’s git doesn’t turn off. In the same way, separators finds a copy of a parser by what it splits on: a call to any function of package strings with + as an argument, as a literal or as a constant, splits or joins an image’s layers, so it belongs in internal/image. A call with another argument that holds a +, such as strings.ContainsAny(arg, "+,"), doesn’t count.

The shared tools have one owner too, the table image.SharedTools in internal/image/tool.go, whose agents’ entries it makes from the coding agents’ registry, agents.Defs (adding a coding agent). Each entry, an image.ToolDef, holds a tool’s name, its kind (a toolchain or an agent), its members (the tools in the lock that its name stands for, such as pnpm and bun for node), the files in a project folder that call for it, and its installer, which is mise for every tool but rust, which rustup installs, and dotnet, which assets/shared-tools/build.sh unpacks from Microsoft’s SDK archive. A toolchain’s entry also holds the environment that every VM’s shells get for it, such as NPM_CONFIG_PREFIX and .NET’s telemetry switch (Env), the folders of the VM’s home that go on every VM’s PATH, where its global installs go (PathDirs), and the members whose version files mise reads in a project (VersionFiles). mise locks dotnet’s version without a download, because its own installer runs Microsoft’s install script, which checks nothing, so devvm adds each platform’s archive and its SHA-512 from Microsoft’s release metadata to the lock (withSDKDownloads in internal/tools/dotnet.go), and Share.Build passes them to build.sh (image.OwnDownload), which checks the archive with devvm-fetch. image.Toolchains, image.Agents, image.GroupTools, the files that make devvm choose a toolchain for a new VM, the lock’s check for downloads (image.NoDownload) and the devcontainer.json features that devvm maps to a toolchain all come from it. So do the files that every launch’s setup writes for the toolchains: /etc/devvm/toolchains.sh, with every toolchain’s environment and PATH folders (image.GuestEnv and image.GuestPath), which base’s /etc/profile.d/devvm-tools.sh reads in every shell, as it reads the agents’ /etc/devvm/agents.sh, and the VM’s mise setting that names the tools whose version files it reads (image.VersionFileTools). The image builds read none of them, so a toolchain’s environment changes no image. The structure test fails on a string literal outside internal/image that is a toolchain’s name or a member’s, whole, so code elsewhere asks the table, through image.Def, an entry’s Installer or its other fields, rather than naming a toolchain. Adding a toolchain and adding a coding agent list the files a new shared tool needs, and the agreement tests fail until the table and those files match.
