The scripts that devvm’s builds run with bash have one owner for the machine they run on, assets/prelude.sh, whose $devvm_arch, $devvm_libc and devvm_sha give each script its architecture, its C library and its pinned checksum for each download (the scripts’ prelude). A script reads them rather than run uname -m or look for apk itself, and checks that the prelude came first with : "${devvm_arch:?}" for each variable it reads, which also tells shellcheck that the variable is set. Go reads each of those scripts through image.OwnScript, which puts the prelude before it, so a recipe, a tool image’s key and the conversion’s copy of oci/build.sh all hold the two together. TestPreludeUsers in internal/image fails when a script that doesn’t get the prelude, such as assets/oci/bootify.sh or assets/guest/’s, uses it, or when a script reads a variable without that check. testdata/script/prelude.txtar checks which pin devvm_sha picks from each script’s pins on arm64 and amd64, with glibc and with musl. A CLI test or a Go test that sources one of these scripts sources assets/prelude.sh first.

internal/paths also owns how a path on the host is resolved and compared with a folder, in resolve.go, whose comment says which resolver each question takes. paths.Physical resolves every symlink as far as the path exists, for where a folder or file really is, such as a project folder against devvm’s own folders or an SSH key against the folders VMs mount. paths.PhysicalParent resolves only the folder’s symlinks and keeps the last element as named, for a path that may itself be a symlink devvm mustn’t follow, such as a key’s recorded path or a Seatbelt rule. filepath.EvalSymlinks itself, which fails when the path doesn’t exist, is for a path that must exist, such as the folder devvm runs in, or a stopped VM’s project folder, which each of a start’s three checks resolves with filepath.EvalSymlinks (an existing VM). Then paths.Within tells whether a path is a folder or inside it, and paths.Below whether it’s inside it only. Both compare names, so both paths are resolved the same way first. A check that keeps a VM away from a folder, such as project.Unsafe’s, an SSH key against the folders VMs mount, or a project folder against an agent’s folder, uses paths.In or paths.Under instead, which also compare the folders themselves and match when the path, or a folder above it, is the same folder as the other, by device and inode. On a volume that ignores case, as macOS’s do by default, ~/.Config/devvm is ~/.config/devvm, which a comparison of names alone misses.

A VM’s state, vm.json, has one owner too, internal/state, which reads and writes the whole file and knows only its core fields. Every other package that keeps something of a VM’s owns one section of it, with its own type, its name (Section), and an Of that reads it through state.Section: internal/netpolicy owns net, internal/gitprotect git, internal/ports ports, internal/sshagent agent, internal/tools tools, internal/secrets secrets, and internal/vm size, clone, devcontainer, desktop and links (internal/vm/state.go). A section’s type keeps what the user asked for at its top level and what devvm made under made. A change goes through state.VM.Update, which takes the VM’s lock, reads the file again, runs the change and writes the file once: the change sets its section with state.SetSection and works out a list’s new value from the file as it is then, never from what the command read earlier, so a change another devvm made meanwhile is kept. A change that fails writes nothing. Update holds one VM’s lock, so a change takes no other lock inside it, and a change to several VMs updates each in turn. Test builds and the tests panic on a lock taken out of that order (the lock rule). state.VM.Claim is Update that also holds the claims lock, for what no two VMs may have (ports.Allocator chooses every VM’s host port through it), and state.VM.Create writes a new VM’s whole state once, its ssh alias chosen under the claims lock. A build VM has no state, so ports.Allocator.Build chooses its ssh port through state.Claims, which holds the claims lock alone. A VM’s alias is one vmname.IsAlias accepts, or devvm doesn’t use it. internal/vm’s checkState reads every section of the folder’s VM’s state as the VM is found, so a section that can’t be read stops the command instead of reading as empty. A new section adds its check there.

Agreement tests

When two places must agree but can’t be one, a test checks that they agree. TestEveryPartHasAPolicy checks that every image part has its policy, TestSharedToolsPolicies that the policies in assets/shared-tools/ are one for each shared tool in image.SharedTools, TestConfigTools that assets/shared-tools/mise.toml lists each shared tool’s members and nothing else, TestBuiltinPolicies that every policy devvm ships parses, TestEveryMessageIsUsed that every message has a caller, TestDocLinks that every doc link is a message and a heading, TestPreludeUsers that only the scripts that get the prelude use it, TestDefsComplete that every coding agent has its [tool_alias] line and its row in the docs’ Supported agents table, TestProvidersComplete that every provider in agents.Providers has its row in the docs’ table of the API keys the proxy puts in, TestToolchainsComplete that every toolchain has files that call for it and its row and section on the toolchains page, which names those files and its PATH folders, TestFormatsCoverLogins that every agent’s login file has its format in internal/agentlogin, TestBumpCoversPins that scripts/bump.sh moves every pin it finds, or says why it’s left (updating pinned versions), and TestReferenceIsCurrent that the CLI reference matches the commands. A new pair of places that must agree gets such a test.

The consolidation pass

A review of a body of work, and the review before a release, look across the code for copies:

  • two parsers of one format
  • a path built outside internal/paths
  • a list of files kept beside the folder that holds them
  • a value encoded in a string
  • two messages that say one thing
  • a comment that says to keep two places in sync
  • a test that copies a constant

Each copy gets one of three outcomes: extend the owner, make one owner, or leave it. Leave it when the only shared helper would be the wrong one, because a copy costs less than the wrong helper, and wait for a third copy before making one. The pass is part of those reviews, not a step every change runs.

Secrets in the code

A value that lets whoever holds it act as you or as a VM is a redact.Secret, from the moment devvm reads it until the place it’s used. That covers a VM’s proxy password (netpolicy.Key, proxy.Config.Password, backend.Confinement.ProxyPassword) and a build proxy’s, a secret’s value (secrets.Store.Value, Get and Save, and what ui.UI.Secret reads), the company proxy’s password and the Proxy-Authorization the proxy sends it, the values the proxy caches for a VM’s bindings (proxy.Lookup), and an agent’s API keys and tokens once they leave its login file (agentlogin.File.Get and SetKey, and the tokens a capture or a refresh brings). Two such values stay strings, as where secret values live explains: the value on its way through platform.KeychainGet and KeychainSet, which secrets.Store makes a Secret at once, and devvm desktop’s VNC password, which you must see. A Secret prints as <redacted> with %v, %s, %q, %x, %#v and every other verb, so a log line, an error or a struct printed with %+v never shows it. Its value is behind a pointer, because fmt prints a value in an unexported field without calling its Format, and such a field then shows only an address. Two Secrets are equal with == only when they’re the same one, so compare their values with Reveal, or the structs that hold them with reflect.DeepEqual.

Reveal is the only way to the value, and forbidigo refuses every call to it except in tests. So each place that must use a value says why in a //nolint:forbidigo // <why> on that line. Those places are the proxy’s password check and the headers it puts values in, the store’s file and the Keychain, the VM’s proxy URL and a login’s file, its refresh and its claims. Anywhere else, pass the Secret on. testdata/lint/forbidigo.go keeps a call to Reveal that the rule must report. The structure test refuses a struct that embeds redact.Secret outside internal/redact, which would take on its methods, and an interface that declares Reveal() string, whose calls forbidigo wouldn’t see. It reads the source alone, so it doesn’t see a Secret embedded through another type or reached through reflection.

Encoding a Secret as JSON or as text is an error (redact.ErrEncode), never <redacted>, so a value written somewhere by accident fails at once rather than losing your login. A file that must hold the real value therefore writes it through its own wire type, a struct with the value as a string that only that file’s reader and writer use:

  • The proxy’s config, proxy.json, is configFile, with Config’s fields in Config’s order, so its bytes, and the Sum that decides whether a running VM’s proxy starts again, match what earlier releases wrote. TestConfigFile holds the two types together.
  • A VM’s key in vm.json is netpolicy.NetMade’s own MarshalJSON and UnmarshalJSON, through netMade.
  • A secret’s file without a Keychain is the value and a line’s end, which secrets.Store.save writes and saved reads.
  • A login’s file is the agent’s own format, read and written whole as a map so that fields devvm doesn’t know stay, and a key or token leaves the map through agentlogin’s token and goes into it through setToken.

To add a field that holds a secret, give it the type redact.Secret. If a struct with it is written to a file, add the field to that file’s wire type, and check that a frozen release’s files still read and write the same bytes: TestV010ProxyConfigs does it for proxy.json, TestFixtureVMStates for vm.json’s sections, TestFixtureStoreGet for a secret’s file on Linux, and TestFixtureAgentStore for the agents’ login files, which every read leaves as they were.

Changing the state layout

State files describes the layout, and the design note says why it’s built that way. Every path in it comes from internal/paths. paths.Dirs names the shared folders and files, and Dirs.VM(name) gives a VM’s paths.VM, whose methods name each file in the VM’s folder: Dirs.VMDir(hash), vms/<hash>/, for a project VM, and run/builds/<name>/ for a build VM. A new file of a VM’s gets a method on paths.VM, so it lands in the VM’s folder, and vmFolders.teardown in internal/vm/teardown.go deletes it with the folder, with no list of files to update. A new socket goes in Dirs.Run(), named by a hash, and TestSocketsFit checks the longest path against paths.SocketMax. A new record that only devvm writes is JSON, read with encoding/json, which ignores fields it doesn’t know, and written whole with state.WriteFile. A new default goes in internal/settings, which reads config.toml strictly and saves settings.json, and a new lock is an OS file lock (platform.LockFile and its kin) on a file that paths names.

The data folder and the config folder each hold a version file with their layout version, state.Layout in internal/state/layout.go. Before each command that reads them, state.CheckLayout takes version.lock in the data folder and compares both files with state.Layout. A folder without the file gets this devvm’s version, the same version goes on, and a newer one stops the command with layout_newer, because a newer devvm changed the folders. An older one runs the migrations from that version to this one, in order, and then writes state.Layout into both files. skipsLayout in internal/cli/root.go lists the commands that skip the check: help, completion, the version and devvm’s own hidden commands.

testdata/script/layout.txtar makes two VMs on the allowlist tier, a forwarded port, a link and a secret, lists every file and folder under the data and config folders, and compares the lists with the ones at the end of the script, one for macOS and one for Linux. A change to the layout, such as a new file, a renamed folder or a file that moves, changes a listing, so the test fails until you update it. When it does, decide whether the change needs a new layout version:

  1. A change that an older devvm would read wrongly, or a file that moves, raises state.Layout by one.
  2. It adds a state.Migration at the end of migrations(), which changes the folders from the version before to the new one. A migration takes paths.Dirs, and a run that it fails stops before the versions change, so the next run tries it again. TestMigrations checks that there’s one migration for each version before this one, and TestCheckLayout runs fake ones.
  3. It updates the listings in layout.txtar.

A new file that an older devvm doesn’t need to know about, or a field added to a JSON file, which an older devvm ignores, keeps the version and changes only the listings.

Released state

Someone who upgrades devvm keeps their VMs, defaults, agent store and secrets as the release they came from left them. Until 1.0, an upgrade from every release since 0.1.0 has to work. Each final release that changed what devvm writes on disk has a frozen copy of the state it left, called its fixture, and the tests run today’s devvm on every fixture, so a change that breaks an older release’s state fails the gate.

What a fixture holds

A release’s fixture is the folder testdata/v<release>/. Its darwin/ folder holds the state that the release left on a Mac, and its linux/ folder the state it left on Linux. For 0.1.0, that’s four VMs’ states, its defaults, its agent store and logins, the stubs’ record of the VMs, and what its --json printed for them, and the folder’s README.md lists what each VM has. The release made these files itself. Its generate.sh checks out the release’s tag in a temporary folder and runs generate.txtar with that version’s own CLI test harness, then copies what the run left, with each file’s mode in modes, because git doesn’t keep modes.

A fixture is frozen. It’s generated once, from the release’s own binary, and never edited or generated again, so never run its generate.sh from a newer devvm and never change its files. A release whose state is the same as the one before it adds no fixture, and neither does a release candidate, such as 0.1.1-rc.1, because only a final release that changes the state gets one.

The tests on every fixture

The unit tests read every fixture’s files with today’s readers. stateFixtures in internal/vm/fixture_test.go lists each release’s expectations: its VMs, the version of their vm.json, its layout version, its clones of one repo, and functions that check its VMs, its defaults and its agent store. 0.1.0’s entry is v010Fixture in fixture_v010_test.go. TestFixtureVMStates, TestFixtureVMsRead, TestFixtureSettings, TestFixtureAgentStore and TestFixtureClonesReadAsOneRepo run once for each release and system, and they check that each field the release wrote reads and writes back unchanged. TestStateFixturesListed fails when a folder in testdata has no entry, or an entry has no folder. Two packages keep a table of their own for what only they read. In internal/proxy, fixtureBinaries records the SHA-256 of the binary that made each release’s state, which its proxy configs name, and TestFixtureBindings and TestFixtureProxyConfig read every release’s bindings files and proxy configs. In internal/secrets, storeFixtures names a secret that each release’s store on Linux keeps as a file, which TestFixtureStoreGet reads through a VM’s binding. TestV010Rules is a copy of 0.1.0’s own tests of the proxy’s rules, kept apart from today’s.

The CLI tests run today’s commands on each fixture. A release’s scripts are in testdata/script/, named fixture_v and the release’s version without its dots, such as fixture_v010.txtar, fixture_v010_clone.txtar and fixture_v010_network.txtar for 0.1.0. Each one puts the state into a sandbox with fixture v<release>, which moves it to the sandbox’s folder: the folder’s path, each VM’s name hash, its folder’s and .git’s identities and its backend’s place become what they are there, each host port, and each port that a VM or the defaults forward, becomes one of the sandbox’s own that nothing on this host listens on, and nothing else changes. The ports change because a launch that finds a VM’s port taken, by a program of yours or by another run of the tests, rightly chooses another one and edits the VM’s Lima config. It also warns that it can’t forward a port that a program has, such as a web server of yours on 3000. A script names a forwarded port by what it was, as $FIXTURE_PORT_3000. The script then runs today’s devvm on it. Each --json must have everything the release’s had (json_superset), the read-only commands must change no file, and a launch must start each VM as it is, without a Lima edit. The scripts stay separate for each release, because their checks name that release’s VMs and what each one has, and TestFixtureScripts in internal/cli fails when a fixture has no script or a script names a fixture that isn’t there.

Changing what devvm does with state

A change that reads or writes state, such as a new command, a new section in vm.json or a new field in a record, runs its new commands on every fixture in the same commit, and reading the files isn’t enough. Add the steps to each release’s scripts, as fixture_v010_network.txtar runs rules by method and path on 0.1.0’s app VM and fixture_v010_clone.txtar runs devvm clone add on its web VM. When a fixture’s test fails, today’s devvm breaks the state that the release’s users have. Fix devvm, or add a migration, but never change the fixture.

A change in what devvm does with existing state gets a line in CHANGELOG.md, in the Unreleased section at the bottom until its release moves it to the top: a step in What to do when the user has to act on it, and otherwise a line in the group of the people who notice it, as Releasing says. When the user has to do something about it, such as run a command, devvm also tells them once, at the first launch after the upgrade.

Freezing a release’s state

At release time, after the tag exists, a final release that changed the state format gets its fixture. A release candidate gets none, even when it changed the state, and its final release’s fixture holds that state:

  1. Copy the newest fixture’s generate.sh, generate.txtar and README.md into testdata/v<release>/. Set the tag, the version and the script’s name in generate.sh, and add the VMs and commands to generate.txtar that make the state the release added.
  2. Run generate.sh on a Mac and on Linux, which writes darwin/ and linux/. 0.1.0’s were made on an arm64 Mac and on x86_64 Fedora.
  3. Add the release’s entries in stateFixtures, fixtureBinaries and storeFixtures, and its scripts, made from the newest release’s scripts with checks of its own VMs.
  4. Commit the folder as the run left it. The older fixtures stay as they are.

The support window

An upgrade from every release since 0.1.0 works until 1.0. When a release leaves the window, its fixture and the code that only its state needs, such as a reader of a field that only that release wrote, go together, in one commit that says which release left and why. The commit deletes testdata/v<release>/, its scripts and its entries in the tables above.

item.title: Backends, toolchains and agents
item.description:
How a backend plugs in

devvm runs every VM on Lima, but the rest of devvm reaches Lima only through the backend.Backend interface in internal/backend, so another backend is an addition rather than a change to the callers. A backend lives in a package of its own under internal/backend, and it does four things:

  • It implements backend.Backend and returns its errors instead of ending the run: a msg.M, or backend.Logged(m) once a logged command failed, so the command shows the run log’s end before the message. Backend is the backend’s Name and Caps and four roles, each an interface of its own that every backend implements in full:

    • backend.Host is what the backend needs of this machine and where it keeps its VMs there. Problems lists what the host lacks for it, and backend.Check(ctx, b) returns the first of them, so a backend doesn’t write a check of its own. NameMax is the longest VM name it takes, Location is where its VMs live when that can change between runs (backend.LocationOf), and DiskDirs and Floors are the folders its disks are in and the free space it wants there (backend.Space). A backend whose VMs can’t move returns "" from Location, and one whose disks aren’t on this machine returns no DiskDirs.
    • backend.Images builds images and the shared tools’ images and keeps the images. BuildImage runs the spec’s Recipe (image.Recipe, which internal/build puts together and image.Input hashes) as it is, each image.Step with its arguments and as root when it says so. Origin is the backend’s own steps that base starts with, such as the Ubuntu image Lima pinned on this machine, a --from image’s conversion, base’s disk size (backend.BaseDiskGiB) and base.yaml. Base’s size is backend.BaseCPUs, backend.BaseMemoryGiB and backend.BaseDiskGiB, never read from a backend’s files. internal/build puts them first in base’s recipe, as its Origin, so base’s key hashes them, and BuildImage is given them back and runs those rather than reading its own files again. PinOrigin pins what base starts from on this machine, which internal/build asks for before it keys a build (backend.PinFirst): on Lima, that’s the newest Ubuntu cloud image (state.UbuntuPin, found by ubuntu.Finder). A base build’s ImageSpec.Packages, a backend.Packages, sends its packages into the VM’s backend.PackagesDir before the steps and takes them out after, which internal/build/packages.go records or replays and checks, and a step that exits backend.ExitUnreachable fails as build_sources_unreachable.
    • backend.Machines makes, starts, stops, renames and deletes VMs, lists them, and runs commands and shells in them. A stopped VM changes only at Start, which first checks with backend.Validate that it can apply the VM’s backend.Want, such as a disk no smaller than the VM’s own, and then applies what the Want asks where it differs from the VM. Start leaves a running VM as it is, and the callers, not the backend, warn that a change waits for the VM’s next start. On Lima, Start owns the config’s env:, propagateProxyEnv, dns and hostResolver, and a project VM’s size, agent mounts and forwardAgent, which it compares with the VM’s before its one edit (what devvm sets on a VM). Ports are never the backend’s: vmssh.Forwards forwards them over the backend’s SSH. Running says how a VM runs now, in one backend.Run: the ID of its current start, whether it’s confined to its proxy, and its lifeline, the file that the VM’s proxy and port forwarder follow. The backend runs no port forwarder of its own, and SSH says how ssh, links and devvm’s forwarder (vmssh.Forwards) reach a running VM’s sshd, a target that vmssh.FromTarget checks. Every ssh of devvm’s to a VM, its port forwarder’s included, refuses a target that isn’t on this machine’s loopback, 127.0.0.1, with vmssh.FromTarget (what each backend emulates). All three get it through vmssh.Checked, which checks the review lets the backend’s ssh through, checks the target, and adds the VM’s host keys for its current start, reading the record (vmssh.ReadKeys) or pinning the keys first (vmssh.PinKeys). A VM whose ssh isn’t usable fails with a *vmssh.UnusableError and one without host keys with vmssh.ErrNoHostKeys, which the ssh config skips on. Exec passes its backend.ExecOpts streams on as they are. When they’re a terminal’s files, the command must get a terminal in the VM, as a shell does, because an agent’s login that draws full-screen needs one, and any other streams are pipes (TestExecStreamsAsGiven on Lima).
    • backend.Housekeeping is what devvm space and devvm gc ask: Usage, Strays, and DevvmCache and DeleteCache for its own caches. A backend that can’t tell returns none.

    backend.Forgetter is the one role a backend may leave out, for the files it keeps for a VM besides the VM. Lima keeps none. Lima’s type, lima.Lima, holds the backend’s fields, Name, Caps and the helpers its roles share, and it embeds one type for each role, host, images, machines and housekeeping, each over the Lima it’s part of. backendtest.Fake is split the same way. So no type has more methods than the structure test allows, and a new method goes on the type of its role.

  • It declares Caps, saying for each of backend.Features whether it has the feature natively, emulates it, or lacks it (features). It lists every feature by hand, None included, and Registry.Register refuses Caps that leave one out or rate a feature better than the one Feature.BuiltOn says it’s built on (Caps.Check). The callers, not the backend, decide what a VM needs, and they check it with the registry’s Review.Require(b, vm, spec.Features()...) before they act. A feature the backend lacks fails in one line that names the VM and what to do, and devvm never falls back to something weaker. An emulation stays refused until its review passes: a design note in the design notes, a threat check with the security-audit skill, and end-to-end checks that prove its guarantee.

  • It’s registered in registry.New (internal/backend/registry), the only place besides internal/cli that imports a backend. The registry hands the backend out behind its guard, which checks every CreateVM, Start, BuildImage and BuildTools call before the backend sees it. The guard refuses a spec that needs a feature Review.Require would refuse, using the specs’ own Features, and a build spec whose ImageSpec.Validate or ToolsSpec.Validate fails, such as one with a network that isn’t a build’s or a key that isn’t one. So a caller that forgets Require still can’t reach a backend with a feature it lacks, and the backend doesn’t check those specs itself. The guard has every role’s methods, its own in place of the backend’s for those calls, so a guarded backend handed on as a backend.Images or a backend.Machines is still guarded. The guard’s type has only backend.Backend’s methods, so code that looks for an optional role, such as backend.Forgetter, uses backend.As instead of a type assertion, and the structure test fails on a type assertion to a backend package’s type anywhere but the guard.

  • It names its images by key, and an image’s key hashes the backend’s name, so two backends never share an image.

  • It passes the conformance suite, backendtest.Conformance(t, factory), which checks the contract that backend.Backend’s documentation gives. The backend’s tests call it with a factory that returns a new backendtest.Subject for each check, and each check runs as a subtest. The subject is the backend, holding one image, whose key is Image, and no VMs. Dir is a folder of the check’s own for the folders its VMs mount, Boots says whether its VMs start, and Restart starts a running VM again outside Start, as a command of the user’s own would. The suite checks every role’s answers and the empty answers each role allows, that a VM is made, renamed and deleted as its spec says, and that a missing VM is backend.ErrNotFound. It also checks that Running gives a stopped VM its lifeline with an empty ID, that every start gets another ID, that a VM is Confined only while it runs on a start Start made with NetProxy, and that the registry’s guard still refuses what the backend lacks when the backend is used as backend.Images or backend.Machines alone. checkProxyURL checks what the open tier needs of every backend, which has no feature of its own (features): a VM on the backend’s own network (NetDirect) reaches a port on the host’s loopback, and the guest’s proxy settings come from the confinement (Confinement.GuestProxy, ProxyURL). When Boots is false, the checks that need a running VM are skipped with the reason, and when Restart is nil, so is the one that needs it. backendtest.Fake runs the suite in internal/backend/backendtest, and TestConformance in internal/backend/lima runs it on Lima twice: on the limactl stub, whose VMs start, and on real Lima’s dummy instances, which can’t boot, so the checks that need a running VM are left to the end-to-end tests. The real Lima run skips when limactl isn’t on PATH. TestConformanceFinds checks the suite itself: each of a set of fakes that breaks the contract in one method fails the check meant to catch it.

The registry’s For chooses a VM’s backend: a VM that exists gets the one its state records in backend=, and a new VM gets backend.Default, which is lima. Tests set the registry’s NewVMs to give new VMs a fake backend (backendtest.Fake). The command line has no way to choose a backend, so a second backend would also add one, following the cli skill, together with its column in the tables that list VMs, images and caches. --json output already names each VM’s, image’s and shared tool’s backend.

A new backend gets a design note and a threat check with the security-audit skill before any of its emulations is marked reviewed, and that check covers what Lima gets from its VMs’ design. A VM started outside devvm must not forward an agent devvm didn’t choose, a VM whose root can change its own network must not count as confined, a secret the proxy needs goes in a private file and never in a command’s arguments, and a socket on this machine goes in a private folder.

Adding a toolchain

Each toolchain is one image.ToolDef entry in image.SharedTools, in internal/image/tool.go, and the rest of devvm reads every list of the toolchains and every fact of one from there: its members in the lock, the files in a project folder that call for it, its installer, the environment that every VM’s shells get, the folders of the VM’s home that go on every VM’s PATH, and the members whose version files mise reads. --tools, devvm tools, the picker, shell completion, the new VM’s summary and the devcontainer.json features that devvm maps list the toolchains from the table too, and every launch writes the environment, the PATH folders and the version files into the VM, so a new toolchain changes no image. A new toolchain that mise installs from the lock’s checked downloads, as it installs node, python and go, needs these files and nothing else:

  • internal/image/tool.go: its entry, with its Env, PathDirs and VersionFiles when it has them.
  • assets/shared-tools/mise.toml: a line in [tools] for each member, with its hold, and a line in [tool_alias] for each member that isn’t one of mise’s own (core:), naming the backend it comes from.
  • assets/shared-tools/<name>.policy: the hosts its allowlist allows, such as its package registry and the downloads of the versions a project asks for.
  • testdata/mise.lock and tests/e2e-mise.lock: each member’s lock entry, which scripts/bump.sh e2e-tools writes into the second.
  • docs/content/docs/using/toolchains.md: its row in the table, in the registry’s order, its section, with what it brings, the files that call for it, its version files, its global installs and its allowlist, and its row in the glibc table of Which bases they run on.
  • tests/e2e/tools_test.go: its checks, such as a project’s VM that its files call for, a global install and a version file’s own version.

Then the golden files in internal/vm/testdata/golden take its environment, its PATH folders and its version files with UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 go test ./internal/vm -run Golden, and a reviewer reads their diff. TestToolchainsComplete, TestToolchainGuest, TestSharedToolsPolicies and TestConfigTools fail until those files match the table, and the structure test fails on a string literal elsewhere that is its name or a member’s.

A toolchain that needs more than mise’s install gets code of its own, which the table can’t hold. A step in each VM, such as rust’s rustup in ~/.cargo, go’s telemetry switch or dotnet’s /etc/dotnet/install_location, is a block of assets/guest/sync.sh that reads the toolchain’s version from the VM’s tool list. An install that mise can’t check, such as rust’s, which rustup checks against its own signed manifest, or dotnet’s, whose SDK archive devvm adds to the lock with its SHA-512, is an Installer of its own, with its branch in assets/shared-tools/build.sh and its handling of the lock in internal/tools.

Adding a coding agent

Each coding agent is one agents.Def in internal/agents/agents.go, and the rest of devvm reads every list of the agents and every fact of one from there: its shared tool (image.SharedTools makes its entry, glibc-only or not), its settings folders and files with each file’s format, its Seeds, its Names and NamedValues, the folder that devvm agent import copies from, its login files and their kinds, its history and what an export leaves out of it, the environment that every VM’s shells get, which turns off its self-update and telemetry, the secret every VM with it uses, how devvm agent login logs it in (its Login: the command lines of its own login, with a code and for a setup token, and whether the login comes back to a forwarded port or you paste a code back; or API keys alone), whether config.toml’s [pass-keys] takes it, and its row in the docs’ Supported agents table (its Docs). Its Seeds are the folders it reads in a VM as a seed of a folder of the VM’s own, such as Claude Code’s plugins. Each one has the link that the VM’s home puts the store’s folder at and the entries that devvm agent import and devvm agent save copy, which agents.MachineOwn judges. Its Names and NamedValues are the tables in its settings files whose keys are names you choose, such as its MCP servers’, which agentlogin.Redact doesn’t judge as keys, read from the agent’s own docs. The commands’ help, --agents, the picker, shell completion, the messages and the CLI tests’ lists of the agents all come from the registry too. A new agent that works like one devvm has needs these files and nothing else:

  • internal/agents/agents.go: its Def and its name’s constant.
  • assets/shared-tools/mise.toml: its line in [tool_alias], the backend it comes from, and in [tools], its version.
  • assets/shared-tools/<name>.policy: the hosts its allowlist allows.
  • testdata/mise.lock and tests/e2e-mise.lock: its lock entry, which scripts/bump.sh e2e-tools writes into the second.
  • docs/content/docs/using/coding-agents.md: a section on its login when it has one.
  • CHANGELOG.md: its entry.
  • tests/e2e/network_test.go: its name in the network section’s --agents list, which launches one VM with every agent, and the checks of its allowlist, its login and its copies there.
  • assets/guest/sync.sh, only when it needs setup in the VM beyond its settings and logins, as Claude Code’s link in ~/.local/bin and Codex’s lines in its config.toml do.
  • When it keeps a login file: a format for each of its kinds in a file of its own in internal/agentlogin, named for the agent, with the format interface’s methods, kind naming its kind (and keyFormat or chatGPTFormat when its Def says it saves API keys or holds a ChatGPT login, and captureFormat when the VM’s proxy captures its logins: its token endpoints, the start of its User-Agent when another agent shares an endpoint, its capture and its reply to the VM’s own refresh), added to the list in formats in format.go, with its fixture in goldenLogins (internal/agentlogin/golden_test.go) and its golden file, and its format’s section in internals/network.md.

Then mise run cli-docs writes the agent’s row in the Supported agents table, its name in the README’s list and the CLI pages whose help lists the agents, and the golden files in internal/vm/testdata/golden take its paths with UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 go test ./internal/vm -run Golden. TestDefsComplete, TestFormatsCoverLogins, TestSharedToolsPolicies, TestConfigTools and TestReferenceIsCurrent fail until those files match the registry. Code of the agent’s own, such as a settings filter or a login of its own, goes in a file named for the agent, such as claude.go or agentlogin_claude.go, and names the agent by its constant in internal/agents, so the code for every agent calls a hook there rather than asking which agent it has. The structure test fails on a string literal elsewhere that is the agent’s name or holds its folder, on code outside the agent’s own files that compares with its constant, has a case for it, looks for it or keys a map on it, on a list in Go that names every agent, tests included, and on a CLI test script’s line that lists agents as a message does, which $AGENT_CHOICES, $LOGIN_AGENTS and $KEY_AGENTS stand in for. The network section of the e2e tests drives every agent, so the new one gets its checks there.

Adding a provider

The model providers whose API keys the VM’s proxy puts in for the agents with a key for each provider, opencode and pi, are one table, agents.Providers in internal/agents/agents.go. Each agents.Provider holds the provider’s ID, which is its entry’s name in both agents’ auth.json, its name as people know it, the hosts the agents send its key to, its Path when the agents send the key below one path of those hosts alone, such as OpenRouter’s /api/, the Headers they send it in, most often one but two for OpenRouter, whose Anthropic models take the key in x-api-key, and its Prefix, which starts the key’s placeholder when an agent checks how the provider’s keys start: pi takes an OpenAI key that doesn’t start with sk- for a Sign in with ChatGPT login, so OpenAI’s is sk-. The opencode and pi formats’ bindings, agentlogin.KeyProviders, which devvm agent login --provider takes and its help lists, and the allowlist lines of each binding’s hosts all come from it. A new provider is its entry there, in the order of its ID, and its row in the table in using/coding-agents.md’s API keys the proxy puts in, which TestProvidersComplete checks against the registry. Read the hosts, the paths, the headers and any check of how a key starts in both agents’ own source first, and in the SDK that each one sends its requests with, because a header that differs from the agents’, or one that an agent uses for some models alone, leaves the key’s placeholder in the request, and a host that the agents never send the key to would get the key anyway. The proxy puts a provider’s key in only when the header’s value is the placeholder alone, or Bearer and the placeholder in Authorization, so check that both agents send the key that way too. A Path starts and ends with /, is clean, and goes into each binding as its Path, below which pathWithin takes a request’s path, so set one only when every request of both agents with the key goes below it. Then mise run cli-docs writes the CLI page whose help lists the providers, and UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 go test ./internal/agentlogin -run Golden writes the golden files that list them.

item.title: The CLI and its messages
item.description:
CLI conventions

devvm’s commands follow one set of rules, so that a user who knows a few of them can guess the rest. A bare verb acts on this folder’s VM, anything else goes under its noun, and a bare noun shows or lists. A setting shows bare, changes with a value and takes -g for what new VMs get. The cli skill holds every rule, with a checklist for adding a command and a review for changing one, and its judgment.md explains, with examples, the rules that only a reviewer can check. The reasoning behind most of them is in the Command Line Interface Guidelines, and Cobra’s own mechanics are in Cobra’s docs.

The tests check every rule that a machine can, and mise run test runs them. The cli skill says which test checks each rule and which rules a reviewer checks by hand, and The CLI rule tests says what each test checks. After changing a command’s Use, Short, Long, Example or flags, run mise run cli-docs and commit the CLI reference it writes.

Each command gets the run’s services from one app, in internal/cli/app.go, which NewRoot makes for the run’s UI and hands to every command’s constructor. The app holds devvm’s folders (dirs), a test build’s overrides, the secrets store, the backends’ registry, the shared tools, the environment of the commands on this folder’s VM (vmEnv) and the image builder of the backend new VMs get (builder, the VM environment’s Builder). It makes each one the first time a command asks for it and keeps that one, or its error, for the rest of the run, so the retention that runs before a command and the command itself share them. A command on this folder’s VM runs in a.env, which returns the command’s failure with its message for an error that isn’t one. A new command takes its services from the app rather than making its own.

A command fails by returning its error from RunE, as failed(err, what) when the error may not be a message: what makes the message from the error’s text, such as msg.LsFailed. execute shows what the command returned in showFailure, and it’s the one place a failure is printed. A backend.LoggedError shows the end of the run log, then its message (ErrorLogged). A message, or an error that carries one, shows as it is, and any other error shows in what’s message, or in output_failed when the command didn’t say what failed. The run then exits with 1, and ui.Main runs the cleanups. Once the run is interrupted, a failure prints nothing, because the interrupt is the reason. The root’s layout check (checkLayout) returns its failure the same way, from PersistentPreRunE. Only the UI ends a run itself, in die, where no command can return: a question that gets no answer, and a run log that can’t be opened.

INT, TERM and HUP cancel the run’s context in ui.Main, which then waits for the logged command that’s running to end. When there are cleanups to run, it also waits for the command’s own code to return, for up to 2 seconds (returnGrace), before it runs them and exits with 130. So a cleanup never undoes a command’s work while that command still runs, and a command that can’t stop delays the exit by no more than those 2 seconds. A question waiting for its answer isn’t waited for at all, because reading its answer doesn’t end at Ctrl+C, and an answer read once the run is interrupted is refused, so nothing goes ahead after it. A run with no cleanups exits at once, because nothing could undo its work, so the proxy and devvm’s other background processes stop as soon as they’re told to. A second signal during the cleanups is ignored, so they aren’t stopped halfway.

Ctrl+C reaches every process in the terminal’s group, so it can end a command that devvm runs before devvm itself sees the interrupt. When a command ends by a signal, or exits with a code of 128 or more, devvm waits up to 1 second for its own interrupt (interruptGrace), so that the run ends as interrupted, printing nothing, instead of showing the command’s failure.

Whatever a failure would leave behind, such as a build VM or a temporary file, registers a cleanup with the UI’s AddCleanup and removes it, with the function AddCleanup returns, once there’s nothing left to clean up. The cleanups run when the run ends, last added first, whether it ended normally, failed or was interrupted. They run after the command returned and the run’s context is canceled, so each one gets a fresh context of its own. A cleanup that only undoes unfinished work after an interrupt checks Interrupted(), and the command leaves it registered once the run is interrupted, because the cleanups run only after the command returns.

devvm runs every external command through the UI’s LoggedCmd(ctx, step, cmd), which a backend gets as its Runner. The command’s output goes to the run log, a terminal’s status line shows step, and a failure after it is returned as backend.Logged(m), which shows the end of the log with the message. WithSteps(ctx, n) starts a phase of n steps, and each LoggedCmd with the context it returns is numbered, as [2/5] running base.sh, on its status line and in the log.

Status lines

Any work that can take noticeable time runs under a status line, so that the user sees what devvm is waiting for. Such work is a host command, host git, a command in a VM, a backend’s own commands, such as limactl list, a request over the network, a walk of a folder the user owns, a lookup of a folder’s disk with macOS’s diskutil, and a wait for a lock, a timeout or another process. A logged command shows its step on its own. Other slow work shows one with the Reporter’s Status, whose label is a message in locales/en.toml: a lowercase phrase in -ing, such as reading_vms, with a description that says what runs under it. For example:

func ListAll(ctx context.Context, e *Env) ([]Listed, []Known, error) {
 defer e.Status(msg.ReadingVMs())()
 inv, err := ReadInventory(ctx, e.Dirs, e.Registry, AllBackends)

The status line shows only in a terminal, without -v and until the run is interrupted, because nothing would clear one started after that. The UI keeps status lines as a stack. A logged command or a Status inside another shows its own line until it ends, and then the UI draws the outer one again, so a phase can show one line around steps that show their own. A message said under a status line, whether Info, Warn, Note or data on Stdout(), clears the line, prints, and draws the line again below it, so a warning never lands on the status line. A question, the picker and ui.Terminal, which a command in the VM that draws on the terminal gets, hold the status line until they’re done, so its redraw never goes over a prompt or what the user types.

A wait for a lock that another devvm holds shows a status line only while it waits, never when the lock is free. platform.LockFile, platform.LockFileShared and platform.LockDir take a platform.Waiting, which they call once they find the lock held, and they call its end once the wait ends. msg.Waiting(status, label) makes one from a Reporter’s Status and a label, such as vm_state_waiting. internal/state, for a VM’s lock or the layout’s, and internal/trust take no Reporter, so they alone take the run’s Status from the context (msg.StatusOf), which the run’s root sets (msg.WithStatus), and forbidigo keeps it to them. The layout’s migration shows layout_migrating while it runs. An agent’s login file is locked by its folder’s lock (platform.LockDir), which the proxy holds while it refreshes the login, so it takes its wait as agentlogin.File’s Waiting (agent_login_waiting), and its wait ends with the caller’s context, as every lock’s does. Only a lock that never waits, such as one on a file just made, passes platform.NoWait, which shows nothing, and the structure test’s status-lines rule holds it to statusSites, as it does a nil. msg.Waiting with no status, as in a process with no UI, gives a wait that shows nothing, never nil. A test build’s locks panic on a nil one (platform.CheckWaiting, which the root’s run calls in every test build), so the CLI tests and the end-to-end tests catch one that the rule can’t see, such as a zero agentlogin.File’s. They don’t catch a msg.Waiting given a nil status, which only a review finds. A forbidigo rule refuses syscall.Flock and unix.Flock outside internal/platform, the proxy’s log rotation, the stubs and tests, so every lock goes through internal/platform’s.

Work that takes the terminal never runs under a status line, because its redraw would go over what the work shows. That work is a VM’s shell, ssh-add asking for a key’s passphrase (checkAgent, Agent.Ensure) and an agent’s login in the VM. A launch shows its status lines around those steps rather than across them. A background process, such as the proxy, a forwarder or a link session, has no terminal and shows none.

Tests check the label rather than a terminal. A msg.Fake gives each status line’s label, and each logged command’s step, to its OnStatus, and Showing returns the one showing. So a seam that the slow work goes through records what showed meanwhile, as TestAgentImportStatus does with the Opencode and ExcludeFromBackup seams, and a backendtest.Fake gives each call to its OnCall. TestLaunchStatusLines runs a new, a running and a stopped VM’s launch and fails on any backend call made with no status line showing, except the shell’s, which takes the terminal, and Running’s, which reads the VM’s pid files. TestCommandStatusLines does the same for the commands that show, list, change, export, stop and delete a running or a stopped VM, including devvm network lock’s picker, devvm restart, the restart that devvm mount-cache asks for, links, and a group with a second VM that runs, stops and goes. It answers their questions in a terminal through the msg.Fake, checks that the picker and the restart are asked, and fails on a question asked under a status line, or a proxy or link session started with none. testProxy runs each link session as a sleep that says each of its links is carried, as its links change. TestVMLockWaits, TestCheckLayoutWaits and each lock’s own test check a wait’s status line. TestSSHAddOffStatusLine fails on an ssh-add that runs under one, on the user’s agent or devvm’s own, and chflagsCalls fails a clone test on a lock or unlock of .git with none. The structure test’s status-lines rule fails on a function that does slow work it knows by name and shows no status line of its own. That slow work is a host command, host git, a walk of a folder, a volume’s lookup, a request through internal/fetch, a wait for a lock that shows nothing, or a backend’s command outside a step. The rule passes a function when statusSites lists it with why, such as the status line of the caller it runs under (The structure test).

Command arguments

Each command checks its arguments and flags before it does anything else, so a usage error never looks for a VM, applies the retention settings or changes a file. internal/cli/args.go holds the checks:

  • A command’s Args is one of noArgs, exactArgs(n), maxArgs(n) and minArgs(n), never Cobra’s own validators, whose errors are in English. Each one names the arguments the command’s Use shows (KEY_FILE, [all|none|LIST]), and with ValidArgs set, it refuses any other value. noArgs on a command with commands of its own says the word isn’t one of them and lists them.
  • Values are checked in Args too. A command adds its own check with cobra.MatchAll, such as settings.ParsePorts for devvm ports or netpolicy.Rule for devvm network allow, returning the same message the command would fail with later.
  • Flag values are checked by name in checkFlagValue, because one flag name has one meaning: --cpus, --memory, --disk, --ports, --lifetime, --older-than, --tools, --agents and --layers. Flags that can’t be given together are marked with exclusive(cmd, a, b), which checkFlags checks first, in place of Cobra’s MarkFlagsMutuallyExclusive alone.
  • The parser’s own flag errors (an unknown flag, one without its value, a value its type refuses) become messages in flagError, set as the root’s SetFlagErrorFunc.

checkCommands wraps every command’s Args in these checks when NewRoot builds the tree. A message one of them returns is a usage error: Execute prints it, then usage_help naming the command’s own --help, and exits with 2. usage_error is only the fallback for a parser error devvm doesn’t know. What a command’s RunE returns once it ran is a failure, which execute shows and exits with 1. TestUsageErrorsEveryCommand runs every command with an unknown flag, without the argument it needs, with too many and with each flag’s value blank, and checks that each is a usage error and nothing runs.

devvm itself takes no arguments, so a layer may have a command’s name. The root’s Args is noArgs, which for the root runs checkWord (internal/cli/word.go): a word that isn’t a command is a usage error. When the word, or each name in it joined with + or a comma, is a part’s name, from the same partNames that checkPartFlag reads (image.Toolchains, image.Agents and the build env’s layers), the error is no_command_part, with the flags that choose them. Any other word gets the closest command, from Cobra’s SuggestionsFor with SuggestionsMinimumDistance 2 (msg.SuggestDistance, which msg.Closest also uses). devvm’s own help command and the root’s help func run the same check, so devvm help WORD and devvm WORD --help fail as devvm WORD does. The help func can’t return an error, so it panics with a wordPanic that execute recovers. --tools, --agents and --layers are checked in checkFlagValue through checkPartFlag: none alone, or a list of the part’s names. A name of another part’s is refused with that part’s flag (part_other_flag), and any other name it doesn’t know with the closest name (vm.CheckPart).

The CLI rule tests

The Go tests in internal/cli walk the command tree, so a command that breaks one of the command line’s rules fails mise run test, whether it’s new or changed. Each exception says why, in its test’s list or in the command’s own about:

  • TestEveryCommandsHelp checks that every command users see has a Short in sentence case without a full stop, a Long of one to three sentences, an Example and a docs page in its about, and that each of the root’s commands is in a group. devvm help is the exception, as Cobra lists it apart and the CLI reference leaves it out. TestAboutGroupsAreHelpGroups checks that each group a command names is one of helpGroups.
  • TestPersistentFlags checks that every command takes -h/--help, --no-input and -v/--verbose and has no other persistent flag. TestFlagNames checks that each shorthand is in its list, -h, -v, -f, -g and -n, for one flag only, that no command takes --yes, and that a flag has one help text wherever it appears, except the names in manyUses. TestFlagNamesHaveOneMeaning checks that a flag name has the same shorthand, type and value everywhere. TestDurationFlags checks that a flag whose value is a DURATION is read with state.ParseDuration in checkFlagValue, and that no flag is a Go time.Duration.
  • TestShowCommandsTakeJSON checks that every command users see takes --json or says why not in its about’s noJSON, and TestJSONShapes checks that every command with --json has a shape.
  • TestCommandNames checks that command names are lower case without aliases, that no command is named list, show, get, delete, remove or ls but devvm ls, that a command named unX has a sibling X, and that each argument in a Use is a PLACEHOLDER or a word, with |, [] and ... only. TestUseMatchesArgs runs every command with the arguments its Use shows, from argSamples, and with none when they’re optional, and checks that it runs, so its Args takes what its help shows. TestUnknownWord checks that devvm WORD, devvm WORD --help and devvm help WORD fail alike for a word that isn’t a command, and that a toolchain’s, an agent’s or a layer’s name, alone or joined with others, points to its flag while any other word gets the closest command.
  • TestCommandLines reads every devvm command line in the repo: the docs, the generated CLI reference among them, the README, AGENTS.md, locales/en.toml, Go’s comments and strings, assets/, install.sh, the CLI tests and their stubs, the scripts, the workflows and the skills. It checks that each one’s command exists, that each flag is one that command takes, that a placeholder is one its Use shows and a flag’s value the one its help shows, such as DURATION, and that a word after a command with commands of its own isn’t a command from elsewhere in the tree. A command line written to be typed, in a code block, a code span or a CLI test’s exec, also has its values checked with checkFlagValue, and when it has nothing to fill in, it runs in a tree whose commands do nothing, where it mustn’t be a usage error. Prose has only its command and its flags checked, because its words after the command are English. The lines written to show a refusal are in refused, each with why, and a CLI test’s ! exec lines are left out, as they’re meant to fail. mise run lint:docs runs it too, so a docs change that names a command that doesn’t exist fails there. TestCheckCommandLine checks that it finds each kind of stale line.
  • TestQuestionsDeclareAnswers in internal/cli finds every question the code makes, outside tests. A question is a msg.Question, which Ask, Confirm, Answer and Secret take, and only two methods of a message make one: AnsweredBy("--force") names the flag or command that answers it, and RefusedWith(msg.X(...)) gives a question that no flag answers the refusal that says what to do instead. The test checks that each AnsweredBy names a string, that each flag in it is one its command takes and each command one devvm has, and that each RefusedWith gives a message, so no question is asked without its answer declared. TestCheckAnswer checks that it finds each kind of wrong answer.

Messages

Every message devvm prints is a table in locales/en.toml, and Go code calls it through a function generated from it. internal/msg renders messages but never prints them; the run’s ui.UI does. Only cmd/devvm and internal/cli hold it. Every other package prints and asks through the one msg.Reporter interface, which ui.UI implements: a package’s type embeds it, its constructor takes it, and cli gives it the run’s UI. A package that takes no Reporter gets the answer instead, because cli asks the question first and passes the answer in. Where a package’s warnings also say where the run log is, as Lima’s and the shared tools’ do, its type has its own Warn method over the Reporter’s. A Go test gives a package a msg.Fake instead, a Reporter that prints nothing and refuses every question unless the test sets its fields, and records what it says with a msg.Recorder.

Prose is never built with fmt: every sentence devvm shows the user is a message. A message made from an error carries that error with .Because(err), rather than only its text from err.Error(). Data output, such as a table or --json, isn’t a message, and neither is text in a script that runs somewhere else. Data goes to the UI’s Stdout(), and a log line that isn’t a message goes to its Stderr().

The locale files are in go-i18n’s TOML format, with only go-i18n’s own message fields, so go-i18n’s loader reads them as they are and its goi18n tools work on them:

[no_vm]
other = "There's no VM for {{.dir}}. Run devvm to make one."

[gc_tools]
one = "{{.count}} shared tool image is unused ({{.size}})."
other = "{{.count}} shared tool images are unused ({{.size}})."

[gc_tools_no_vm]
description = "tools lists the tool images, as \"node 24.21.0, claude 2.1.295\""
one = "{{.count}} current shared tool image no VM has ({{.size}}): {{.tools}}."
other = "{{.count}} current shared tool images no VM has ({{.size}}): {{.tools}}."
  • The ID is the table’s name, in snake_case.
  • other is the text: a Go template whose fields are snake_case ({{.vm_name}}). Only plain fields are allowed, no logic.
  • Fields’ types: the generator makes each field a string parameter of the message’s function, except count, which is an int, and vm and vm_name, which are vmname.VM. A field that may hold something other than a VM’s name, such as an image’s name or a VM’s name as the user typed it, is named what or name instead.
  • one is the text for a count of 1, when the wording changes with the count. Both texts then take {{.count}}.
  • description is an optional note for translators.
  • Nothing else: the generator refuses keys go-i18n doesn’t know, nested tables, plural forms English doesn’t use (zero, two, few, many) and leftDelim/rightDelim.
  • Voice: a message’s text follows the docs-voice skill’s Messages rules, which set its length (an error or a warning has at most two sentences, and a prompt at most two lines of context), and the mechanism goes in its doc link rather than its text.
  • One line: a value renders on one line without control, bidi or invisible characters, because msg.OneLine cleans every value as the message renders. Text from a VM that devvm shows as data goes through msg.Printable instead, which keeps its newlines and tabs. Colors says what the two drop.

Doc links

A message links a docs page through the docs map in internal/msg/docs.go, from message ID to a page in docs/content/docs and a heading on it. The page is its path without .md, and a section’s own page, its _index.md, is the section’s folder:

var docs = map[string]string{
 "vm_outdated": "using/images#outdated-vms",
 "backend_lacks": "backends#when-a-backend-lacks-something",
}

devvm prints the page’s address on the docs site on the line after the text.

After editing en.toml, run:

mise exec -- go generate ./internal/msg

It writes internal/msg/messages_gen.go, with one function per message. The parameters are the template’s fields in sorted order, in camelCase, and count int for plural messages: [no_vm] becomes msg.NoVM(dir string) msg.M, and a value that’s missing or extra is a compile error. msg.M is also an error: one made from another error carries it with .Because(err), so errors.Is and errors.As see through it, while the text stays the message’s own.

The tests fail when:

  • messages_gen.go is stale;
  • a message doesn’t render with sample values, or shows <no value>;
  • a generated function is never called outside the generated file and the tests;
  • a doc link names a message that isn’t in en.toml, or a page or heading that doesn’t exist. mise run lint runs this check too.

Questions

A prompt asks a msg.Question, never a bare message, so every question declares what answers it where devvm can’t ask: without a terminal, with --no-input, or once the input ends. A message becomes a question in one of two ways. msg.X(...).AnsweredBy("--force") names the flag or command that answers it, and its refusal is no_input, which names that answer and shows the question first when the prompt wasn’t printed. RefusedWith(msg.Y(...)) makes a question that no flag answers, and its refusal is the message given, which says what to do instead. About(...) adds the messages said before the question, which devvm shows only when it asks.

The Reporter’s Ask, Confirm, Answer and Secret take the question and, where devvm can’t ask it, return its *msg.Refusal, an error whose Msg is the refusal’s message. A command returns it as it would any failure, and a caller with something to fall back on does that instead, so no caller checks for a terminal itself. TestQuestionsDeclareAnswers checks every question in the code, as The CLI rule tests says, and a CLI test answers one with ttyin or DEVVM_PIPED_ANSWERS=1, as CLI tests says.

Names mode

With DEVVM_MESSAGES=names, a message prints as its ID and its values in sorted key order, so tests check which message devvm printed and with what, never its wording or language:

! exec devvm _msg nope
stderr 'msg_unknown name=nope$'

Every CLI test runs in names mode unless it sets env DEVVM_MESSAGES=.

Names mode belongs to internal/ui, which reads it once, with the rest of a stream’s style, in New: a msg.M itself always renders as its text, so its String and Error are the same whatever the environment says. Whatever shows a message as data, a table’s cell or a --json field, goes through the UI’s Text, or a Table’s, to get the names in names mode. New takes the function it reads the environment with, os.Getenv for devvm’s own UI, so a Go test makes a UI in names mode without setting the environment and can run in parallel; cli’s testUI does. A Go test that checks a message without a UI compares Names, msg.IDOf or msg.NamesOf.

devvm _msg NAME key=value… prints a message’s text (never its names), for end-to-end tests that look for it in a VM’s output. It’s hidden from the help.

Colors

Only internal/ui adds color, through a style for each stream that onTerminal makes, and colorOn decides each one: NO_COLOR or DEVVM_MESSAGES=names turns it off, then FORCE_COLOR or CLICOLOR_FORCE (but 0) turns it on, then TERM=dumb turns it off, and otherwise the stream gets color only when it’s a terminal. Names mode stays plain in a terminal too, so end-to-end checks that run devvm under script read the names as they are. A UI from New, as tests make, has no terminal, so it’s plain unless the environment it reads sets FORCE_COLOR or CLICOLOR_FORCE, which is how cli’s tests get a colored one.

The colors are SGR codes from the 16 base colors only, which the theme maps to its own shades. devvm uses no bright colors (90–97), because Solarized maps them to greys and bright black is Solarized Dark’s background, and it uses no backgrounds, 256 colors or truecolor. The codes go on labels, links, log text and a message’s values, never on the template’s own words:

  • A message’s values are bold (1), on the status line and in prompts too. msg.M.Segments renders the template with each value between two private-use runes, U+E000 and U+E001, after dropping those runes from the values, so a value can’t start or end a marking of its own. It returns the text cut into segments, each one the template’s words or a value, beside the doc link. Joined, the segments are Text, and String and names mode don’t change. Every value goes through msg.OneLine as the message renders, in Text, Segments and Names alike, so a value has no newline or other control character, whoever made it, bold or not. The log end that ErrorLogged prints is the message on one line without bold, because bold inside dim would cancel it.
  • Error’s devvm: label is bold red (1;31), and Warn’s is bold yellow (1;33).
  • A doc link is underlined blue (4;34). msg.M.Segments gives the doc link apart from the text, so ui colors the link alone.
  • Info’s ==> is bold (1).
  • The run log’s end that ErrorLogged prints, with its --- lines, the log text on the status line, and the log’s lines that -v streams (SetVerbose: LoggedCmd and LogWriter copy the log to stderr through msg.Printable, with no status line) are dim (2).
  • The done mark that a slow step leaves is green (32).

The codes are added after msg.Printable and msg.OneLine, so they’re the only ones devvm prints. Those two are devvm’s one cleaner, and msg.Safe is its one rule for which characters reach the terminal. They drop every character that msg.Safe refuses but newline and tab (which OneLine drops too), and a lone C1 byte. msg.Safe takes a graphic character in any script, such as an accented letter, a CJK character or an emoji, so a VM’s file names still read as they are. It refuses the control characters (C0, DEL and C1), the bidi controls such as U+202E, which reorder the text after them so a name could read as another, the format characters, such as the zero-width space and joiners, the word joiner, the soft hyphen and the tag characters, the variation selectors, and the fillers that show as nothing, such as U+3164 and the braille blank U+2800, which could hide or fake text in a prompt. The diff of devvm agent save writes each character that msg.Safe refuses as its code instead, and the names of the files it saves must hold none. The status line, the run log’s end, Pick, devvm network log and the port forwarder’s log use them as well. The status line cuts and counts its plain text with style.fit before painting it, so it still fits the terminal’s width and clears the right number of rows. The run log is never colored.

Tables on Stdout() are colored as stdout is. A command gets a ui.Table from u.Table() and adds a header, rows of ui.Cells and a totals row, and cli never reads the environment itself. Each cell has a ui.Role: Good is green (32), Attention yellow (33), Bad red (31), Secondary dim (2), and Plain stays in the default color, while the header and totals rows are bold. Table pads each cell on its plain text before painting it, because text/tabwriter counts the codes’ bytes as width, and a plain table is byte for byte what text/tabwriter writes with a padding of 2 (TestTableLikeTabwriter). The roles for each table’s values are next to the code that writes it:

  • devvm images: current is good, stale, unfinished, unused and not built need attention, and digests and keys are secondary.
  • devvm ls: Running and the .git protections on and clone are good, Stopped needs attention, and any other status, such as Broken, is bad, as is the tier unenforced, while a confined tier, internet, allowlist or none, is good and open stays plain.
  • devvm space: only copy and leftover in KEPT need attention.
  • devvm doctor: native is good, emulated needs attention, and unreviewed and none are bad.

Every command’s --json output is for scripts and stays plain.

mise run test unsets NO_COLOR, FORCE_COLOR and CLICOLOR_FORCE, and the end-to-end tests unset the last two, so your own settings never change what they check.

Translations

A translation is locales/<language>.toml (de.toml) with the same tables, one and other translated (and the language’s other plural forms, such as few), loaded by go-i18n the same way. Doc links are the same in every language: the docs site is English. devvm picks the language from the first of LC_ALL, LC_MESSAGES and LANG that is set (de_DE.UTF-8 is German); C and POSIX are English. A message missing from a translation is shown in English.

JSON output

Every command that shows or lists something takes --json, which jsonFlag in internal/cli/json.go adds. The command builds a struct of its own with snake_case json tags, next to the code that writes its table, and writes it with printJSON, which puts "version": 1 (jsonVersion) first, writes HTML characters as they are and refuses anything but an object. A list it prints is never nil, so it’s [] rather than null, and a field that doesn’t apply is omitempty. Sizes are bytes unless the field’s name gives the unit, as in memory_gib.

The root command’s PersistentPreRun calls u.DataOnly() for any command given --json, so Say, Info and LogNote print to stderr from then on, and stdout gets only the JSON. A settings command that also changes its setting with a value wraps its Args in showsOnly, which refuses the value with --json (json_shows_only) before anything else runs.

TestJSONShapes in internal/cli/json_test.go holds each command’s shape, a path: type line for each field of a sample with every field set. A field renamed, removed or given another type fails it. Shapes only gain fields, so a new field goes into the sample and the test, and any other change raises jsonVersion. A new command that shows or lists something gets --json, a row in that test, a CLI test and a section on its page with an example, which output for scripts links to.

item.title: Tests
item.description:
Go test helpers

Every change to devvm’s logic comes with a test, and Go tests are table tests next to the code they test. Neither the Go tests nor the CLI tests touch the Keychain, real VMs or your own folders. A Go test that writes state points the XDG folders at t.TempDir(), and a Go test makes VMs only on the fake backend, backendtest. The CLI tests run the built devvm against the stubs, so only the end-to-end tests make real VMs. The Go tests share a few helpers, so each one reads the same way:

  • stubtest.New(t) puts the stubs first on PATH for one test, as the CLI tests have them, with a new folder under /tmp as their STUB_DIR and its calls file as their STUB_LOG. The folder goes when the test ends. stubtest.New(t, "ssh") puts only the stubs it names on PATH, so the host’s other commands, such as git, stay. Its Calls returns the calls the stubs logged, Reset forgets them, and Touch, Write and Read work on the files the stubs read, such as a switch, a file whose presence makes a stub fail. VM, Size and VMs set and read Lima’s instances in the stubs’ state, and Keychain and SetKeychain the Keychain’s items. stubtest.Command(t, "mise") returns the path of one stub, for a test that runs it by its path, as DEVVM_HOST_MISE does.
  • stubtest.Git(ctx, args...) is plain git for a test’s own repo, and a test runs git only through it, which the structure test checks. Its environment is the test’s without git’s variables that pick a repo, its files or its config, such as GIT_DIR, GIT_WORK_TREE and GIT_CONFIG_PARAMETERS (stubtest.GitEnv), and it reads no global or system config. A git that runs the tests, such as a hook’s or git rebase --exec’s, sets some of those variables, and a test’s git that kept them would work on the checkout itself, writing its config and commits there. A test that runs something else that runs git, such as a script or a stub, calls stubtest.NoGitRepo(t) first, which takes the same variables out of the test’s environment until it ends, and stubtest.New calls it for the stubs. The CLI tests’ environment leaves them out too.
  • stubtest.ExecRunner is a backend’s runner that runs each command as it is, with no run log, so a backend under test runs the stubs.
  • msg.IDOf(err) returns the ID of the message an error carries, or "" when it carries none, and msg.NamesOf(err) returns the message’s names, as names mode prints them, or the error’s own text when it isn’t a message. A test compares either with what it expects.
  • A msg.Fake is the msg.Reporter a package under test prints and asks through. Its zero value is quiet: it prints nothing, has no terminal, so it refuses every question as the UI does where it can’t ask, and runs a logged command as it is. Its fields change that: OnInfo, OnWarn and the other On funcs are given each message or question of their kind, with a question’s context going to OnNote first, OnAny every message, and Terminal, Picks, Interrupt and the writers stand for the terminal, the picker, an interrupt and the output. OnStatus is given each status line’s label and each logged command’s step, and Showing returns the one showing now, for a test that checks slow work runs under its status line (status lines).
  • A msg.Recorder keeps the messages it’s given. Set a msg.Fake’s OnInfo or OnWarn to the recorder’s Add, then compare its Names or its IDs.
  • backendtest.Stored is the fake backend with its disks on the host, for the free-space checks.
  • The proxy’s child in a test’s process gets IO’s confine, a confinement that confines nothing (noConfine), because confineChild would confine the test’s whole process on Linux. ChildMain uses confineChild only when the field is nil, and runChildOn refuses to start without one. A test of confineChild’s own logic calls confineWith with a confinement of its own. A test’s server made with newServer looks up its names and connects in the test’s process, because newChildServer gives it the broker itself. The tests that run the child over a real socketpair (inProcess) send every lookup and connection through the broker instead, and a broker in a test connects through a seam of its own (broker.net’s connect) wherever it could reach the internet. internal/landlock’s TestSelf runs the test binary again as a child that confines itself and logs what it could still do. It runs only without cgo (CGO_ENABLED=0), as CI’s nocgo job and a hand run on a Linux host do, and skips under the race detector, whose cgo keeps Go from reaching every thread. The CLI tests’ devvm is built without cgo, so on Linux their VMs’ proxies’ children run confined too.

Goroutine leaks

A goroutine that outlives its test is one that would outlive its command in devvm, such as a tunnel the proxy carries after it has closed, or a goroutine that passes signals on after its child has ended. internal/leaktest finds them in every package that starts goroutines: internal/proxy, vmssh, daemon, desktop, ui, vm, backend/lima, platform, cli, gitprotect, vmlog and memnet. It imports only the standard library, so the proxy’s and the daemon’s tests use it too.

  • leaktest.Main(m), in a package’s TestMain, runs the tests and, once they’ve passed, reads every goroutine’s stack. It gives the goroutines that are still ending, such as a closed listener’s accept loop, five seconds, then fails the test binary with the stacks of any still running. It leaves out the standard library’s own goroutines that outlive every test and that no test can end, which allowed lists with why: signal.Notify’s loop and an HTTP client’s idle connections. It then reads Go’s goroutineleak profile, which names each goroutine blocked for good on a channel, a lock or a wait group that nothing still running can reach, and fails on any it names. A TestMain that makes the test binary a helper process runs the helper first and calls leaktest.Main last.
  • leaktest.Check(t), called first in a test, fails that test when a goroutine started while it ran is still running once it has ended, its context cancelled and its cleanups run, after the same five seconds. It counts the goroutines the test started, and theirs, followed through those still running, so a test running in parallel doesn’t count. Nor does a goroutine that a server shared between tests starts for the test, such as a server that TestMain or a sync.Once started. That goroutine leads back to the server’s own goroutine, which ran before the test, and Main finds such goroutines at the end. Check’s failure names the test, where Main’s names only the binary, so a test of something that starts and stops goroutines, such as a link session, the port forwarder or the desktop’s relay, calls it.

Anything Main or Check finds is a leak to fix, with a test that fails without the fix. Only a goroutine that the standard library starts and that outlives every test goes in allowed. A new package that starts goroutines gets a main_test.go that calls leaktest.Main, which the structure test checks, and the structure test also lists every goroutine devvm’s code starts, with what waits for it to end (goroutineSites).

Time and lifecycles

A test of a timeout, a grace or a close, such as the relay’s grace, the forwarder’s close or the proxy’s ClientHello deadline, runs in a testing/synctest bubble, synctest.Test(t, func(t *testing.T) { … }), rather than sleeping on the real clock. Inside the bubble, time is fake and moves only when every goroutine of the test is blocked, so time.Sleep(30 * time.Second) returns at once, and synctest.Wait() returns once every other goroutine has done what it can. Such a test takes no time, and a loaded CI machine can’t make it fail, so it never needs the margins a real-clock test does.

A test checks that something happens at the moment it’s due and not a nanosecond before. It sleeps to just short of the moment, calls synctest.Wait() and checks, then sleeps the last nanosecond and checks again. A goroutine that never ends fails the bubble as a deadlock, and a test of something that starts and stops goroutines calls leaktest.Check(t) before the bubble as well.

Time moves only while each goroutine waits on something inside the bubble: a channel, a timer, time.Sleep, a sync.Cond or a wait group. A socket’s read, a process’s wait or any system call that blocks keeps it from moving, so the code under test gets seams. Like every test seam, each one is a field that a test sets to a stand-in in memory:

  • internal/memnet is a network in memory for tests. memnet.Pipe() makes a connection, and a memnet.Network holds listeners by address, whose Listen, Dial and DialContext stand in for a socket’s. Its connections close their writing side alone (CloseWrite), as TCP’s do and net.Pipe’s don’t. They hold up to 64 KiB that the other end hasn’t read before a write waits, as a socket’s buffer does. They have deadlines on the bubble’s clock, and so do its listeners, through SetDeadline. It uses only the standard library, so the proxy’s tests use it.
  • The forwarder and the link sessions take their listeners from their Listen fields, so a test gives them a memnet.Network’s.
