  • The relays carry each connection through an sshRelay, whose start field starts its ssh -W. In production it’s execSSH, and a test’s stand-in, memSSH, is a VM in memory that sends what the test tells it and ends only when its context does, as exec.CommandContext kills ssh.
  • The proxy connects to the far ends through its egress’s connect field, which memServe points at a memnet.Network while it serves the proxy on a listener in memory.
  • A daemon.Proc asks its Alive, Args and Signal fields about its process, so a test of Stop gives it a process table of its own (fakeProc).
  • A test’s own HTTP server, when the test sends the requests itself, is httptest.NewTestServer’s, which serves in memory, and the test sends through its Client(), which reaches it whatever the request’s host.

A stand-in can’t show what the real thing does with a kernel’s buffers, a real ssh or a real process, so each kind of lifecycle keeps one test that runs the real one, on the real clock: TestPipeSSHGrace, TestPipeSSHGraceSlowClient and TestPipeSSHGraceWriteError run the relay with an ssh stand-in on PATH, TestForwarderEndsStuckRelay closes a forward whose relay’s ssh never ends, TestLinksBurst fills a link’s real Unix socket, TestSpliceKeepsAnEarlyAnswer splices over TCP and TestProcStop stops real processes. A new seam keeps the real test of its kind.

The proxy’s tests that start a whole proxy, such as TestMainRuns and TestAgentRelay, run its child in the test’s process (inProcess), on real sockets, so they can’t run in a bubble. Their broker waits testStartWait, 30 seconds, for the child to say it’s ready, through IO’s startWait field, where devvm’s own proxy waits 4 seconds, and each test waits as long for the proxy to listen (retryFor). Under the race detector on a loaded Linux host, those starts can take more than 4 seconds, most of it spent hashing the test’s executable, which each broker does as it starts, so a wait of 4 seconds would fail them.

CLI tests

CLI tests are testscript scripts in testdata/script/*.txtar, run by internal/cli/script_test.go against a freshly built devvm. Call it with exec devvm …:

# An unknown flag fails.
! exec devvm --nope
stderr '^devvm: flag_unknown command=devvm flag=--nope$'

Scripts see messages by their names, so the example checks which message devvm printed, not its wording. A script that checks a message’s text sets env DEVVM_MESSAGES= first.

Run one script with mise exec -- go test ./internal/cli -run TestScript/<name>.

Each script runs in a sandbox under /tmp, never the real folders:

Variable Points to
HOME home/
XDG_DATA_HOME data/
XDG_CONFIG_HOME config/
DEVVM_LIMA_HOME, LIMA_HOME lima/ (short, for Lima’s socket paths)
DATA, VMS, RUN devvm’s data folder, data/devvm/, and its vms/ and run/ folders
CFG devvm’s config folder, config/devvm/
DEVVM_MESSAGES names, so messages print as their names
STUB_DIR stub/, for stubs’ state
STUB_LOG stub/calls, the stubs’ call log
DEVVM_SECRET_SERVICE devvm-test, the Keychain service name
DEVVM_UBUNTU_URL ubuntu/, with a dated release as Ubuntu signed it
DEVVM_KVM stub/kvm, a file standing in for Linux’s /dev/kvm
DEVVM_TEST_CPUS, DEVVM_TEST_MEMORY_GIB, DEVVM_TEST_FREE_GIB 8, 16 and 500: a large host, whatever runs the tests (details)
DEVVM_HOST_MISE the mise stub, which resolves the shared tools in place of devvm’s own mise
DEVVM_CLIP_TOOLS the stubs’ folder, so devvm paste runs the clipboard stubs in place of the system’s tools, such as macOS’s /usr/bin/osascript, and no script reaches the real clipboard
MISE_STUB_LOCK testdata/mise.lock, the lock the mise stub writes
TOOLCHAINS, AGENTS the toolchains’ and the coding agents’ names, in the registries’ order and joined with spaces, as devvm’s messages list them, so a script that checks a list names no toolchain or agent itself (stderr 'names='$TOOLCHAINS'$')
AGENT_CHOICES, LOGIN_AGENTS, KEY_AGENTS every agent’s name, those that devvm agent login logs in, and those with a key for each provider, in the registry’s order and joined with a comma and a space, as a message of choices lists them (stderr 'choices='$AGENT_CHOICES' command=')
DEVVM_BIN the folder of the built devvm, alone
DEVVM_REPO the checkout, for the scripts in scripts/, which tests copy into a throwaway repo before running, and the scripts in assets/, which tests source to check their pieces
DEVVM_SSH_PORTS, SANDBOX_PORT_NEXT, SANDBOX_PORT_END, DEVVM_PORT_RANGE the sandbox’s own ports, as the next paragraph says

Each sandbox has a block of 160 ports of its own, between 10000 and 19999, below both the range devvm chooses ports from and the system’s ephemeral range, so neither a devvm that a script runs nor an outgoing connection takes one. The sandbox holds the block’s lock file in /tmp/devvm-test-ports-<uid>/, a folder of your user’s alone, while it lasts, so no other sandbox has the same block, whether it’s in the same test process or in another one running at once, such as a second worktree’s gate. While every block is held, a new sandbox waits for one, up to 5 minutes. The block’s first 60 ports are for the scripts. The VMs’ ssh ports (DEVVM_SSH_PORTS) come first, and then the ports for free_port VAR… and the fixtures. Each of those is taken in turn from SANDBOX_PORT_NEXT up to SANDBOX_PORT_END, and it’s free on every address, 127.0.0.1 included, when it’s taken (free_port -range FIRST LAST takes two in a row). The other 100 are the range the sandbox’s devvm chooses its VMs’ proxy and desktop ports from (DEVVM_PORT_RANGE, which only a test build reads), so two sandboxes’ devvms never choose the same port.

The built devvm is a test build, so it reads the stand-ins above that a release ignores, such as DEVVM_KVM and DEVVM_HOST_MISE. A script answers a question in one of two ways: ttyin -stdin FILE gives the next exec a terminal whose input is the file, so devvm asks as it does in yours, and env DEVVM_PIPED_ANSWERS=1 with stdin FILE has each question read its answer as a line of the file instead, without its prompt. Without either, devvm has no terminal, so it refuses every question, as a script’s devvm does. It has the checkout’s assets/ embedded, as a release has, and no test build reads them from elsewhere: a script that needs other files for devvm (layers, features, policies) puts them in the user’s folders in the sandbox, as a user would.

$WORK, the script’s own folder, is the current folder. project NAME makes the folder $WORK/NAME and goes to it, as a project’s folder, and project NAME git makes it a git repo too. Once devvm has made the folder’s VM, vm_name VAR NAME finds it among the states in $VMS and sets $VAR to the VM’s name, which ends in an ID the test can’t know, so a script can pass it to a stub (exec limactl stop $WEB). It also sets $VAR_dir to the VM’s folder, $VMS/<hash>, so a script reads the VM’s state as $WEB_dir/vm.json and its network log as $WEB_dir/logs/network.jsonl. catg GLOB prints the one file a glob matches, and fails when the glob matches none or more than one, so a check never reads two files by mistake. vm_state GLOB prints the one VM state a glob matches as sorted KEY=VALUE lines for stdout to match: a section’s fields are dotted (net.on=true, ports.host.ssh=23456), a list of strings is joined with spaces (tools.names=node claude), a list of objects is indexed (links.links.0.name=db), and anything but a string is JSON. Negated, ! catg GLOB and ! vm_name VAR NAME pass when there isn’t exactly one. json_set GLOB KEY=VALUE… sets string fields in each JSON file the glob matches and keeps the rest, or makes the file when a glob without wildcards matches none. KEY:=JSON sets any JSON value, and a dotted key sets a field of an object, which it makes when it’s missing. Scripts write devvm’s JSON records with it, such as a tool image’s record (json_set $SHARE/node-*.json built=2020-01-01T00:00:00Z), because a record’s times are in the file, where touch can’t change them. renumber FILE changes a VM’s state as a boot that numbered the disks’ devices anew leaves it, as macOS does. The folder’s identity and each .git’s git_id get another device, with their inodes and birth times as they were, and $FOLDER_ID and $GIT_ID hold the folder’s and its own .git’s identities from before the change. fixture VERSION puts a release’s state into the sandbox, and json_superset [-shape] [-changes PATH] WANT GOT checks that one JSON file has everything another has, as Released state says. A VM state a script writes as a fixture needs version, id, name, image, dir and backend, created for a VM whose creation finished, and a hash of its own for its folder (json_set $VMS/12345612345601/vm.json version:=1 id=x name=devvm-live-12345612345601 image=base dir=/p/live backend=lima created=2020-01-01T00:00:00Z net.on:=false).

Tests never touch the network. Downloads are served from a test server (net/http/httptest) or read from a file:// folder. DEVVM_UBUNTU_URL replaces https://cloud-images.ubuntu.com/releases/resolute, where devvm finds Ubuntu’s dated releases: point it at a folder of release-YYYYMMDD/ folders, each with its SHA256SUMS and SHA256SUMS.gpg, as file:///path/to/folder. The CLI tests serve internal/ubuntu/testdata/resolute, a release as Ubuntu published and signed it, and Go tests sign their own releases with a key they make (internal/ubuntu/pgp_test.go). devvm’s own releases, which devvm upgrade installs, come from internal/upgrade/upgradetest: a TLS test server laid out as GitHub’s releases, with a minisign key of the test’s own that signs each release’s SHA256SUMS as minisign does. A script starts one with release_server [-badsig] LATEST [VERSION...], which serves a release of each version, the first the newest, each devvm in it a script that prints its version, and with -badsig signs them with another key. It points a test build at the server with DEVVM_REPO_URL, at its key with DEVVM_RELEASE_KEY and at its certificate with DEVVM_RELEASE_CA, and DEVVM_TEST_VERSION gives the test build a release’s version. Container registries (--from) are a TLS test server in Go tests; scripts use pinned digests, which need no lookup, or set HTTPS_PROXY to a closed port, so lookups fail as offline ones do.

A command left running in the background (exec devvm … &name&) can be interrupted with kill -INT name. wait_file FILE waits up to 60 seconds for a file to appear, such as one a stub writes when it gets somewhere, and fails at once when every background command has ended. For anything else, wait_until SCRIPT runs sh -c SCRIPT every 100 ms until it succeeds, for up to 90 seconds. It fails at once when every background command has ended, or when SCRIPT exits 100, which is how a check that can no longer succeed says so, as when it waits on a session that ended. Wait with these two rather than a loop of your own. A script that runs a copy of devvm makes it with cp_exe SRC DST, not cp: on Linux, a command another script starts while the copy is being written keeps the file open for writing until it runs, so running the copy then fails with “text file busy”, and cp_exe writes the file while no command can start.

Stubs

The stubs stand in for every host command devvm runs, so tests never run the real tools: limactl, docker, security, ssh, ssh-add, ssh-agent, ssh-keygen, qemu-img, qemu-system-aarch64, qemu-system-x86_64, chflags, tmutil, sw_vers, uname, open, code, mise, and the clipboard tools wl-paste, wl-copy, xclip, osascript and pbcopy, which read a clipboard the test lays out in $STUB_DIR (clip-types, clip, clip-file) and write what’s copied to $STUB_DIR/copied. They are one Go program, internal/stubtest/stub, which does what the command it’s run as would do: the binary is named stub, each command’s name is a link to it, and it reads its name from its argv[0]. internal/stubtest builds it once, into $TMPDIR/devvm-stubs-<hash> with its links, where the hash covers the stub’s sources and Go’s version. Every test process, and every later run until the sources change, finds that folder and uses it, so the binary builds only once, and a folder of an older build is removed once it’s a day old. TestScript puts that folder on PATH right after devvm’s, ahead of the real commands.

Each stub logs its call to $STUB_LOG as one line, its name and its arguments joined by spaces. The stub writes the line itself, in one write to the log opened for appending, so lines from stubs running at once never mix, and its arguments never go to another process’s command line. That matters because endpoint security tools such as CrowdStrike Falcon kill a process whose arguments look like an ssh option next to a proxy URL with a password, which is what a start’s limactl edit passes. stub_calls prints the log for stdout or cmp to check, ! stub_calls fails if anything was logged, and stub_reset empties the log, so the next check sees only the calls after it:

exec devvm …
stub_calls
cmp stdout calls
-- calls --
limactl list

uname and sw_vers pretend to be another host when these are set, and run the real command otherwise:

Variable Printed by
STUB_UNAME_S uname -s
STUB_UNAME_M uname -m
STUB_SW_VERS sw_vers -productVersion

What the stubs keep between their calls is their state, $STUB_DIR/state.json, which internal/stubtest/stubstate reads and writes as typed JSON under a file lock, so stubs running at once never lose each other’s changes. It holds Lima’s instances, each with its status, size and config, the Keychain’s items, the SSH agent and its keys, and Time Machine’s exclusions. Scripts read and change it with the stub command, and Go tests with the stubtest.Stubs methods VM, Size, VMs, Keychain and SetKeychain:

Command What it does
stub vm NAME STATUS Lima lists the instance NAME in STATUS, such as Stopped, Running or Broken, with Lima’s default size when it’s new
stub vms prints Lima’s instances, one NAME STATUS line each, sorted
stub size NAME CPUS MEMORY DISK gives an instance its size, with the memory and disk in bytes
stub keychain ACCOUNT prints the Keychain’s item for ACCOUNT, and fails when there’s none
stub keychain-set ACCOUNT saves the item for ACCOUNT from its input, so the value is in no process’s arguments
stub agent prints the SSH agent’s keys as ssh-add -l lists them, and fails when no agent runs
stub agent-stop stops the SSH agent
stub names prints every stub’s name

A switch is a file a test makes in $STUB_DIR to change what a stub does, such as start-fails, which makes limactl start fail. The comment above each stub’s function lists its switches, and every switch is named for the command and what happens to it: -fails, -hangs, -fails-on and -waits-on, where an -on switch holds the text that a call’s arguments must contain. A stub that hangs touches $STUB_DIR/hanging first, so wait_file can wait for it. The files a stub writes in $STUB_DIR are what a test checks, such as $STUB_DIR/sync.tar, what a VM’s setup was sent.

limactl keeps its instances in the state and fails or hangs on request. It keeps each instance’s size and config as create, clone and edit set them, and a contract test checks that it does so as real Lima does. Its shell reaches the guest, the VM the stubs make believe in, which ssh reaches too. One module, guest.go, answers whatever devvm runs in a VM, with one set of switches whichever way devvm gets there. limactl shell is also the shell devvm opens in a VM, which then ends, so a script sees it as devvm’s last call. In the shared tools’ build VM, its shell writes the images build.sh is asked for into the build’s folder (or, on request, a symlink instead), and it keeps what a VM’s setup is sent as $STUB_DIR/sync.tar. A base build’s packages go in as $STUB_DIR/packages-in.tar, and what the build gives back is $STUB_DIR/packages-out.tar, or no packages. In the --from build VM, its shell writes what oci/build.sh would (or, on request, a hostile disk, command line, C library or symlink), and a call naming $STUB_DIR/interrupt-on’s text interrupts devvm, as Ctrl+C would. The VM’s ssh host keys are one made-up key for each VM, unless $STUB_DIR/hostkeys-fails exists.

docker stands in only for what --from asks of it. It has an image only when $STUB_DIR/docker-image holds its ID, its save writes a tarball naming that image (or $STUB_DIR/docker-saved’s, a tag that moved), and it isn’t running when $STUB_DIR/docker-down exists. ssh answers a port forwarder’s master with $STUB_DIR/guest-ports, and a link session’s master listens on its control socket. Either master outlives the process that started it, as ssh’s does, until the sandbox’s cleanup stops it or 5 minutes pass. A direct connection from a VM (the self-check’s) fails, as a confined VM’s does, unless $STUB_DIR/net-direct exists. A --clone VM’s git and its seed’s scripts run on the host, with real bash, git and tar, on $STUB_DIR/vmfs/<folder>, and ssh fetches from there (it fails with $STUB_DIR/ssh-fails). A clone’s command fails, as any shell does, when $STUB_DIR/shell-fails-on holds text its arguments hold, such as index-pack for the seed’s apply. security stands in for the Keychain and tmutil for Time Machine, both keeping their items in the state, never in the real ones. mise writes $MISE_STUB_LOCK as the lock ($MISE_STUB_OLDER_LOCK for a list of versions), lists $MISE_STUB_VERSIONS, and fails like mise offline with MISE_STUB_FAIL set. chflags sets no flags, so .git protection leaves test folders deletable. qemu-img and QEMU are there so Linux hosts pass devvm’s checks.

To add a stub, write its function in internal/stubtest/stub, with a comment that says what it does and lists its switches, and add it to stubs() under the command’s name. It logs its call with c.log() first, keeps what it must remember in the state through c.update, and reads its switches with c.on and c.text. A new command the state needs goes in control. To add a switch, read it in the stub’s function, name it for what it does as above, and add it to that function’s comment. Each stub has unit tests in stub_test.go, which run it in the test’s own process. Where a stub prints what devvm parses, such as limactl list --json, the golden fixtures check that it prints what the real tool prints.

devvm runs in $WORK or a folder made in it (mkdir, then cd), never in HOME or devvm’s own folders, which it refuses as project folders.

Coverage

mise run test measures each package’s test coverage, then fails when a package’s coverage is more than a point below its line in the baseline, so coverage only goes up. That point of room is there because the same tests can cover a little less from one run to the next, with timing or the tools a machine has installed. A package inside it passes and keeps its line. Each system has a baseline of its own, testdata/coverage/darwin.txt and testdata/coverage/linux.txt, because macOS and Linux run different code and skip different tests. On a system without one, mise run test says so and checks nothing. A package’s coverage counts its own Go tests and the CLI tests together. scripts/test.sh sets CLI_GOCOVERDIR, so TestScript builds devvm with -cover for every package of devvm’s, and each devvm a script runs writes its counters to that script’s own folder inside it. Scripts run in parallel, and devvm runs that started at the same moment in one folder would race to write the same meta-data file, so one of them would print coverage meta-data emit failed on stderr and fail any script that checks it. go tool covdata then merges every script’s folder with the Go tests’ own counters. That way internal/cli, and code that only the CLI tests reach, such as a backend’s real runner, count as tested. The end-to-end tests don’t count.

When a change raises a package’s coverage, raise its baseline in the same commit. Run mise run coverage, which runs the tests as mise run test does, then writes each package’s coverage to this system’s baseline where it went up, and commit the file. A change that raises coverage on both systems raises both baselines, so run it on a Linux host too. It never lowers a line: a package within a point below its baseline keeps the line it has, and when a package is more than a point below, it fails and writes nothing. A new package gets its line from mise run coverage too, and a package that’s gone loses its line there, because mise run test fails on both until then. coverage.txtar checks scripts/coverage.sh, which compares the coverage with the baseline.

There’s no target percentage: a package is judged by what’s untested in it, not by its number.

End-to-end tests

mise run e2e runs devvm against real VMs, so it needs Lima and takes minutes: run it in the background. It runs TestE2E in tests/e2e, with the run’s flags after --. First it checks that this machine has every command the chosen sections use, and it names each one that’s missing with what installs it (the list). Then it builds devvm from the checkout into its sandbox, its files embedded, and runs every check through that binary:
Lima home ~/.lt-e2e-go (or $DEVVM_E2E_LIMA_HOME); it refuses ~/.lima and devvm’s own
State /tmp/devvm-go-e2e (XDG_DATA_HOME, XDG_CONFIG_HOME)
Keychain service devvm-go-e2e (DEVVM_SECRET_SERVICE), fake tokens only, deleted at the end
Lock /tmp/devvm-go-e2e.lock, a symlink to the pid of the run that holds it, so only one run uses the sandbox at a time
Git identity GIT_AUTHOR_* and GIT_COMMITTER_* of its own, so the harness’s commits and tags work on a machine with no git config, and yours never goes into them; devvm’s own git ignores them 
mise run e2e # every section but desktop and from
mise run e2e -- --from # every section, from too, and base with every feature: the longest
mise run e2e -- --only images,gc # just these sections
mise run e2e -- --clean # delete the sandbox's cached images and tool images first
mise run e2e -- --every-feature # base with every feature, as a run with from builds it
mise run e2e -- --slots 3 # the sections spread over 3 sandboxes that run at once
mise run e2e -- --slot 1 # run in slot 1's sandbox, its images as it has them
mise run e2e -- --newest-base # base from Ubuntu's newest image and packages, in a sandbox of its own
mise run e2e -- --golden # also capture the stubs' golden fixtures from the real tools

End-to-end tests in Go says how to run go test yourself, write a check and add a section.

A change that touches VMs passes the sections for what it changed, with --only, and a run with --only that names from builds base with every feature, as --from does. Before you merge a change to assets/ or to --from, run --from, because only it runs every section on base with every feature. GitHub’s hosted runners can’t run the end-to-end tests on macOS, so a Mac of your own runs them there.

--newest-base builds base as a user’s first build does, in place of the pinned release that the other runs use, and Maintaining says when to run it and what to do when it fails. --golden writes the golden fixtures of this system into the checkout, for you to commit.

The sections so far:

  • images: building base and fixture layers, rebuilds, a failed script and Ctrl+C during a build, then base’s recorded packages, each in the cache under its SHA-256, and base built again under the same key with ubuntu-mirror set to an address nothing answers on, whose apt reads only the build’s own folder of packages.
  • project: devvm in a new project folder (under /tmp/devvm-go-e2e/p) makes a VM from base and opens a shell there, which reads its commands from devvm’s input. The folder and the shared tools are mounted and nothing else is, there’s no SSH agent, no Docker (no docker layer) and the hostname is the folder’s. The ssh config lists it as devvm-web with its host keys pinned; through an ~/.ssh/config of the run’s own that includes it under a Host * forwarding the agent, ssh devvm-web works, forwards no agent (a throwaway one), and refuses a changed host key. .git is locked (macOS) and git in the VM can still commit. devvm stop stops it and drops its entry, and on macOS reports and locks a submodule git folder the VM added. With stand-in clipboard tools in DEVVM_CLIP_TOOLS, devvm paste --json puts the copied image into the running VM’s paste folder, where its SHA-256 matches, mode 600 in a folder of mode 700, and the stand-in copier got the path; devvm paste rm --force deletes it and leaves a file of the user’s; and a stopped VM is refused before the clipboard is read. TestE2EExecQuoting in internal/backend/registry, which runs only there (DEVVM_E2E_VM names the VM), checks that arguments with spaces, quotes, $, newlines and globs, a folder and input reach the guest as given, through the Exec of the backend the VM’s state records, so one test covers every backend. Then a VM from a devcontainer.json, with no ports by default: its forwardPorts said and not forwarded, none reaching this machine, its containerEnv in the shell and its commands, its postCreateCommand run once in the folder, its postStartCommand at each start (again after devvm restart), nothing written to the folder, and a changed file warned about without changing the VM. Then a claude VM with a fake agent config, history, git identity and token in a home of its own: devvm agent import copies the agent’s settings into the sandbox’s agent store without the history or the links out of its folder, naming each link it leaves out, and with config.toml’s follow-links naming a dotfiles folder, it copies the skill folder a link leads to there as a folder, never a link, and still none of the links to a file outside it. The store’s folder is mounted read-only and linked into the VM’s home, the linked skill’s copy with it, which root can’t write either, and the home folder’s isn’t mounted, its settings are copied and its history isn’t, the VM gets the git identity, the timezone and its hostname, and, open as it is, the token’s placeholder and never the token. devvm agent save without a terminal shows the VM’s changed settings.json as a diff and its new commands folder’s file, then refuses and saves nothing, and after a yes it saves both into the store, but neither the VM’s fake login beside them nor the folder’s link out of it. Then SSH agents, with a home of their own and throwaway keys: a --ssh-agent VM uses a throwaway agent standing for yours; after devvm ssh-agent add and devvm ssh-agent devvm it keeps yours, in its shell and by name, until a restart, then uses only devvm’s own agent’s key, in its shells and by name; after devvm ssh-agent off, none.
  • clone: --clone with a throwaway repo, and host git and devvm run with a home of the section’s own, so neither reads your ~/.ssh/config or your git settings, and the Include line isn’t offered. The VM has its own clone with every branch, even though the repo’s url.*.insteadOf sends its URL elsewhere, only the shared tools are mounted, and its shell opens in the clone. The repo gets a devvm remote named after the VM, and nothing of .git is locked or watched. Without a terminal, devvm rm --force refuses while the clone has commits that weren’t fetched and keeps the VM. Once git fetch devvm through devvm’s ssh config has brought the VM’s commit, devvm rm refuses for uncommitted changes in the clone, and then for those in a worktree in the clone, shown under its path, and devvm rm --no-clone-check deletes the VM after a warning, the worktree’s change with it, and removes the remote, while the fetched work stays as a local branch. A git worktree’s VM gets a clone of only its branch and that branch’s upstream. On a VM that mounts its folder, devvm clone on without a terminal is refused, and devvm clone shows off. devvm clone on --force then makes it again with its own clone of every branch, only the shared tools mounted and .git unlocked, and it keeps its home and its ID. devvm clone off --force without a terminal refuses while the clone has commits that weren’t fetched and keeps the clone, and once they’re fetched, it mounts the folder again with .git protected, keeps the VM’s home and ID, removes the remote and leaves the work as a local branch. Last, devvm --clone --repos all in a folder of repos gives one VM a clone of each repo at its path, with every branch, the folder’s own file, and nothing mounted but the shared tools. devvm clone fetch brings both repos’ work back and lists the branch with both repos, devvm clone add copies a third repo into the VM at its path, with a remote, devvm rm without a terminal refuses for the work in one repo that wasn’t fetched, naming that repo, and devvm rm --no-clone-check deletes the VM and removes each repo’s remote. A repo with a detached HEAD, an annotated tag, origin’s branches and an older VM’s remote gets a clone detached at the same commit, with the tag still annotated and origin’s branches, and none of the VM remote’s. The same repo’s staged, unstaged and intent-to-add changes and a tracked file turned into a folder give the same git status in the VM, which has neither the untracked .env nor the folder, and devvm names the folder. Every section but tools uses the shared tools’ versions pinned in tests/e2e-mise.lock, for both architectures’ glibc and musl VMs, and the --from checks start from container images pinned by digest in tests/e2e/from_test.go (fromNodeDigest, fromAlpineDigest and fromUbuntuDigest). The images built from them stay valid until a pin moves. base starts from the dated release of Ubuntu’s cloud image that e2eUbuntuRelease in tests/e2e/sandbox_test.go names, given to devvm as DEVVM_UBUNTU_RELEASE, in place of the newest that a user’s devvm pins, so base’s key stays the same between runs and on every machine of one architecture. devvm keeps a release it has pinned, so when the sandbox’s pin names another release, as it does after scripts/bump.sh e2e-ubuntu moves e2eUbuntuRelease, the run deletes that pin before its first section, and the next build pins e2eUbuntuRelease. Its packages are those its key recorded at its first build in the sandbox, which stay in the sandbox’s package cache through --clean, so base built again under the same key installs the same packages until assets/ or the release changes its key. scripts/bump.sh e2e-tools moves the lock to upstream’s newest versions, resolved with devvm’s pinned host mise, scripts/bump.sh e2e-from moves the digests to what Docker Hub has for each tag, and scripts/bump.sh e2e-ubuntu moves the release to the newest Ubuntu lists; scripts/bump.sh --check shows them against upstream. The lock’s first line is the SHA-256 of the assets/shared-tools/mise.toml it was resolved from, and a run stops at once when that file has changed since, until scripts/bump.sh e2e-tools resolves the lock again.

base, the --from bases and the shared tool images stay cached between runs, except what a rebuild or gc deletes: every stale image in the sandbox (other selections’ bases, whose features differ, among them) and every unused tool image (an earlier from run’s musl ones, and the tools section’s newest versions where they differ from the pins); every other VM a run makes is deleted at its end, and its project folders are unlocked and deleted. Each check prints [n/N], how long it took and the time left as the last complete run of each of its sections measured it, and a heartbeat every minute shows the latest output. e2e keeps each section’s times in a file of its own in slot 0’s state folder, timings/plain/SECTION, or timings/features/SECTION for a run whose base has every feature, because that run also checks base’s features. So a run of any selection, in any slot, estimates from and compares with the sections it runs. A check fails on its first failure, except the few marked Flaky, which flake on timing, such as the network section’s check that the proxy’s password was in no host process’s arguments, and the link section’s 256-connection check and its stopped-target check. When one of these fails, e2e shows its output and runs it once more, and a second failure fails it. Its result says retried once, its line in the timings has a third field, retried, and the summary counts the retried checks and names each one. A check a run has nothing for is counted as SKIP: base’s features, with base cached. A section that runs fewer checks than its last complete run with the same tests/e2e Go files fails the run, because an error ended it early, and e2e keeps the times it had. After you edit those files, each section’s first complete run sets the count the next runs compare with. Checks look for devvm’s messages with devvm _msg, never by their wording. The Go tests that need a real VM or desktop, TestE2EExecQuoting, TestE2ESelfCheck and TestE2EDesktop, skip unless their DEVVM_E2E_* variables are set, and e2e runs each of them through s.GoE2E, which sets those variables in the test’s environment, so a value such as the desktop’s password is in no process’s arguments.

Each check’s command has a time limit, counted from when it starts: three times the check’s longest time in its section’s last complete run, at least 2 minutes, or 10 minutes for a check with no time yet. The checks that build base or a --from base, which Builds() marks, get at least an hour, because their last time may have been a cached build. The steps between two checks, such as the launches that build tool images, get an hour too. When a check runs past its limit, the heartbeat stops the processes it started, with TERM as Ctrl+C would and then KILL 30 seconds later, and the check fails with the heartbeat’s last line in its output. When the steps before a check run past their limit, the heartbeat stops their processes the same way, and that check fails without running. Either way, the run goes on to the next check and then to its usual cleanup.

Slots

A host with spare cores and memory can run the sections at once, each set in a sandbox of its own called a slot. mise run e2e -- --slots N spreads the chosen sections over N slots, from 1 to 9, and runs each slot as a --slot K run of its own, all at the same time. The default is one slot, which is the run described above. Slot 0 is the sandbox in the table, and slot K adds -K to its Lima home, state folder, Keychain service and lock, as ~/.lt-e2e-go-1, /tmp/devvm-go-e2e-1, devvm-go-e2e-1 and /tmp/devvm-go-e2e-1.lock. Each fixed port the checks use is slot 0’s plus 100 times the slot, so slot 1’s servers use 47260 where slot 0’s use 47160. Slot 0’s ports run from 47160 to 47199, from 47240 to 47249, and 47613, 18765 and 18766, so no two slots ever share one.

e2e places the longest sections first, each in the slot with the least time so far, using each section’s time from its last complete run. A section that has never run gets a guess, from 2 minutes for gc and clone to 30 minutes for from. link always goes in the same slot as from when both run, because in the --from tier link’s Alpine client starts from the image that from builds. Each slot runs its own sections in the usual order, and a slot left without a section isn’t started. When go isn’t on your PATH, e2e finds mise’s Go once and puts its folder first on the slots’ PATH, because slots that each ran mise exec at the same time would each install the repo’s tools over one another. With --from, e2e passes --every-feature to every slot, so each slot’s base has every feature, as a single --from run’s has.

Before the slots start, e2e takes every slot’s lock and gives each other slot what slot 0 has and it lacks: every image’s Lima instance and record, every tool image and its record, and devvm’s caches. It clones the large files and never copies them whole: on macOS each one is an APFS clone, which needs both folders on one APFS volume, and on Linux a reflink. The records and the --from digests are small files, so e2e copies them. When a file can’t be cloned, as on a Linux host whose /tmp is tmpfs, e2e says so and that slot builds its own. With --clean, nothing is cloned, and each slot deletes its own cached images instead. A --slot K run of your own uses that slot’s images as they are.

Each slot’s output appears as it comes, each line led by its slot’s number, such as [1], and stays in the slot’s e2e.log. When every slot has ended, e2e prints each slot’s sections, results and time, then the sums: checks passed, failed, skipped and retried, the failed checks by name, and the time the whole run took. The run fails when any slot fails or ends without its results. TERM or Ctrl+C stops every slot with TERM, and each one cleans up as a single run does.

Testing on other hosts says how many slots each kind of host runs. Testing on other hosts also covers Linux hosts, x86_64 and the checks to run by hand.

The tests behind How it works

The How it works pages say in words what the tests of a mechanism check, and this section names those tests, so you can find the one to extend when you change the mechanism. Each unit test is named with its package, the CLI tests are files in testdata/script/, and the end-to-end checks are in tests/e2e, in the section the page names. The design notes name the tests of each emulation themselves (design notes).

  • How the proxy puts secrets in:
    • TestCheckName, TestCheckHost, TestCheckHeader, TestCheckEnv, TestCheckPrefix, TestDefine and TestChangeApply, in internal/secrets, check what a secret of yours may be and what devvm secret set’s flags change.
    • TestReservedEnvAssets and TestEnvReservedForSecrets, in internal/netpolicy, check the variables a secret can’t take.
    • TestInjectSecretShapes and TestSchemeOK, in internal/proxy, check each shape a value goes in and each that keeps the placeholder, and TestPathWithin, TestForRequestMethods and TestInterceptSecretMethods that a binding’s path and methods let it in only for the requests they match.
    • TestGetChecksTheBinding checks that a binding that isn’t the secret’s as it’s saved gets nothing, TestValueMax and TestKeychainLine, in internal/platform, that a value too long for the Keychain’s line is refused, and TestPlaceholders the placeholders’ one shape.
    • TestCustomStore, TestCustomsUnreadable and TestWriteFilesCustom check the list, its mode and its checks, TestValuesCachedByBinding, in internal/proxy, that two bindings of one name are cached apart, and TestCustomSecrets, in internal/vm, use, a new value and the question before a delete.
    • The CLI tests are secret_custom.txtar and layout.txtar, and the end-to-end checks are in tests/e2e’s network section.
  • The VM’s CA: TestInitCA, TestInitCASwitch, TestInitCAReplaced, TestInitCATogether and TestInitCACancelled, in internal/trust, TestPrepareOpen, in internal/netpolicy, and TestNextCASigns, TestLoadCA and TestServersApart. The CLI tests are network.txtar, sync.txtar and layout.txtar.
  • Logins made in a VM:
    • TestCaptureLogin, TestCapturePaths, TestCaptureEarlyHintsAnswerAndSaved, TestCaptureErrorPasses, TestCaptureRefuses and TestCaptureGet, in internal/proxy, check what goes out, what the VM gets and what’s refused.
    • TestCodexCapture, TestOpencodeCapture, TestClaudeCapture, TestClaudeSetupToken, TestClaudeOAuthGet, TestCaptureRefuses, TestEndpoints and TestPick, in internal/agentlogin, check each agent’s file, its placeholders and copies, and its refresh.
    • TestOneClaudeLogin, TestClaudeBindings and TestClaudeOAuthVMCopy, in internal/secrets, check the one Claude Code login and its bindings, and TestCapturer and TestCaptureOwnAgents, in internal/netpolicy, the endpoints in every VM’s config and which agent a capture is.
    • TestAgentLoginTerminal, in internal/vm, and TestTerminal, in internal/ui, check that an agent’s login gets the terminal’s files only when devvm’s input and output are both terminals. The end-to-end checks are in tests/e2e’s network section.
  • Agents’ logins and settings: TestFormatsWithholdUnknown plants a field that no format knows in every login file, ~/.claude.json included, and checks that no VM’s copy holds it.
  • Learning from the log: TestTickable checks that no name devvm network lock ticks is a shared-hosting domain or under one.
  • A company’s CA in builds: tests/e2e’s images section checks that a layer built with a test CA trusts it while its script runs and keeps its key once the folder is emptied, and that a copy of its image booted without devvm has none of devvm’s CA files. Its project and tools sections check a company’s CA in a VM, which tests/e2e runs on real VMs.

item.title: Writing docs
item.description:
Writing docs

The site is Hugo with the Hextra theme, built from docs/. Hextra is a Hugo module pinned in docs/go.mod; update it with hugo mod get github.com/imfing/hextra@<version> in docs/.

  • Pages are Markdown files in docs/content/docs/, one per topic, in a folder per section of the sidebar. The sections run in the order a new user needs them: getting-started/, using/, releases/, safety/, backends/, compared/, cli/, internals/, then contributing/. Each folder’s _index.md is the section’s own page, which lists its pages. Update the page for any behavior you change, in the same change. The README stays high level: it says what devvm is and links to the pages for the rest.
  • What goes where: the user pages, in getting-started/, using/, safety/, backends/ and compared/, say what devvm does, what you type and what you see, and they name no repo paths, Go identifiers or message names. How it works, in internals/, explains how devvm does it, for readers who want to check a claim, and it holds the mechanisms and the message names that come from them. Contributing, in contributing/, covers changing devvm, so repo paths, Go identifiers, version bumps, releases and tests go there, and so do the design notes, which say why devvm is built as it is and hold each emulation’s design note and threat check. A user page links once to its How it works page where there is one.
  • Current behavior, but for releases: every page describes how devvm works now, and none mentions older behavior, what changed or what moved, because that goes in the changelog and on the release pages. Releases, in releases/, is the one place the docs describe history. It has a page for each minor release, such as releases/0.2.0.md, which covers the release and its release candidates and is written as the release is made. Each change there has a section of its own, under Breaking changes, Changes, Fixes or Hardening, that tells its full story: what was wrong or missing, how it showed, how devvm works now, at the level of the user pages, and what you do, with links to the user or How it works pages for anything deeper. The changelog’s entry links each section, as Releasing says. These pages follow the docs voice, but they aren’t user pages, so the rules for leading with a command don’t apply.
  • User pages lead with doing: a task on a user page, in getting-started/, using/, safety/, backends/ or compared/, shows its command, in a copyable block or numbered steps, and a short explanation follows. One paragraph of why next to its command is fine, but two or more paragraphs back to back mean the mechanism belongs on the How it works page, under a heading that the user page links to, with every fact moved rather than dropped. The docs-voice skill’s SKILL.md has the rule, under Commands first on user pages, with an example, and its scan.sh -p paras and scan.sh -p long list the runs and the long paragraphs.
  • Front matter sets title, shown as the page’s heading, weight, the page’s place in its section, or a section’s place in the sidebar for an _index.md, and explainer, the line under the title on the page’s social card, which Social cards below describes. Start the body at ##.
  • Links to other pages point at their files ([Contributing](_index.md)), so the linters can check them.
  • Diagrams are Mermaid code blocks, fenced with mermaid, which a script draws as SVGs before Hugo builds the site, so no page loads Mermaid or any other diagram JavaScript. A diagram goes where it helps the reader follow the text, with at most one sentence to introduce it, and the text keeps every fact the diagram shows.
    • Drawing them: mise run docs:diagrams installs pele with npm ci --ignore-scripts, at the version and integrity that docs/package.json and docs/package-lock.json pin, and then runs docs/render-diagrams.mjs. The script draws each block in docs/content as an SVG in docs/.build/diagrams/, which git ignores, with a JSON file of the diagram’s size beside it. It names both files for the block’s key, which is a hash of the salt and the block’s text. The salt is a hash of pele’s version and the script itself, and the script writes it to that folder too. mise run docs and mise run lint:docs run it first, and so do the Docs workflow’s builds.
    • Caching: a run with nothing changed takes a few hundredths of a second. mise skips the task when the drawings’ folder is newer than every page in docs/content, the script, docs/package.json and the lock, so the script updates the folder’s time on every run. The task runs npm ci only when the lock’s SHA-256 differs from the one it wrote to docs/node_modules/.devvm-lock-sha256 after its last install. The script keeps every drawing that’s already there, draws only the blocks it has no drawing of, and deletes the files no block’s key names, so a changed diagram is drawn again on its own, and a new pele or a change to the script draws them all again. The CI workflow’s check job caches npm’s downloads, keyed on the lock, and the Docs workflow, which publishes, keeps no cache and draws every diagram.
    • Putting them in pages: hugo.yaml mounts that folder at assets/diagrams, and the render hook, docs/layouts/_markup/render-codeblock-mermaid.html, which takes the place of Hextra’s, reads the salt, computes each block’s key from it and the block’s text, and puts the SVG in the page. A block without its SVG fails the build, so run mise run docs:diagrams again after you change a diagram, even while mise run docs serves the site, because the server doesn’t redraw them.
    • The theme is in custom.css, which sets pele’s --pele-* variables from the site’s palette, so a diagram never sets its own colors or font. Panels are on the surface color with blue borders, lines and arrows are lime, subgraphs, lifelines and notes use the border color, and text is in Departure Mono at 14px, larger than the home page’s art so labels read easily.
    • The layout is pele’s own, with the Mermaid settings that render-diagrams.mjs passes, such as right-angled edges. A diagram can set its own layout in front matter, as Staying safe’s three columns set minNodeWidth, but never its own colors or font. pele lays subgraphs out from left to right in the order they’re written.
    • Measuring labels: the script measures each label by Departure Mono’s metrics, where every character is 350/550 of the font size wide, so labels fit their boxes. pele draws edge labels, messages and notes at seven-eighths of the size, 12px, and has no option to change it, so the measurer gives that text its width at 14px and the script then writes it at 14px. A self-check, before anything is drawn, fails the run when pele no longer measures and writes that text as the script expects, and every group of small text that pele draws must carry the 12px size the script replaces. The script also puts a newline after each label, where the SVG draws nothing, so the site’s search sees one label’s last word apart from the next label’s first.
    • Size: each diagram is drawn at its own size and never scaled to fit. The hook sets each diagram’s width on it, and a diagram wider than the text reaches into the page’s right margin, the article’s padding, as far as it needs, and into the padding on the left for whatever the right margin can’t hold, so it never covers the table of contents. A diagram wider than the text and both paddings scrolls sideways, as the widest ones do on a narrow screen. custom.css gives each one content-visibility: auto, so the browser draws it only when it nears the screen, and the hook sets the diagram’s height as its contain-intrinsic-block-size, so the page doesn’t jump while you scroll.
    • Accessibility: every diagram has an accTitle and a one-line accDescr, which become the SVG’s title and description that screen readers read, and the script fails on a diagram without them. The description says in full sentences what the diagram shows.
    • Labels: keep labels short, and break a long one with <br>. In a label, write < as #lt; and > as #gt;.
    • pele’s version is pinned exactly, and scripts/bump.sh pele moves it (updating pinned versions).
  • Style: succinct and direct. Commands are written as devvm x or in backticks, never in quotes. No please, simply or note that.
  • The home page is docs/content/_index.md, on Hextra’s hextra-home layout: its hero shortcodes, then plain Markdown. custom.css styles it through the one div that the layout wraps its content in. After the hero, the page has a quick start, what’s supported, why to use devvm with its feature cards, a short FAQ, and a closing call to action with the hero’s buttons. It keeps a marketing tone, but each of its claims matches the docs page it links to, it uses the same terms, and it says each thing once.
  • The quick start shows the three commands to run first, each after a comment short enough to fit a phone’s width, because a comment after its command would scroll out of view there.
  • Feature cards on the home page come from two shortcodes in docs/layouts/_shortcodes/, which make a {{< features >}} grid of {{< feature title="Ready in seconds" icon="high-voltage" art="copies" >}} cards, each closed with {{< /feature >}}. A card shows its title as a heading, after the pixel icon its icon names, drawn in the title’s own color at 24px, then the Markdown inside it, then its illustration, which is optional. The cards are in one centered column on smaller screens. From 1024px wide, they go into two columns, the first, third and so on on the left and the rest on the right, and each card is as tall as its content, so no card leaves a gap under it. features places them: feature renders its card through docs/layouts/_partials/feature-card.html and hands it over, and each card’s order style keeps the page’s order when the columns stack. What’s supported uses the same cards with smaller illustrations, and Quick start uses them with a terminal in each card. {{< features columns="3" >}} puts three in a row from 1024px wide, and level="3" on a card makes its title an h3, under the section’s own heading.
  • Art beside a section’s text comes from {{< beside art="blast-radius" >}}, closed with {{< /beside >}}, in docs/layouts/_shortcodes/beside.html. It renders the Markdown inside it, then the illustration it names. From 1024px wide, the text and the drawing each take half the column, with the drawing on the right, centered on the text. On narrower screens, the drawing goes below the text. Why use devvm? uses it.
  • Install commands come from {{< install >}} in docs/layouts/_shortcodes/install.html, which the home page and Installing use. The commands are written in one place, docs/layouts/_partials/install-tabs.html, which the tabs and the pages’ Markdown copies both read. It renders Hextra’s tabs with a macOS tab, which has the Homebrew command, and a Linux tab, which has the install script. The macOS tab is selected in the HTML, so it shows when JavaScript is off. A small script in docs/layouts/_partials/install-os.html selects the Linux tab as the page loads when the browser’s platform or user agent string says Linux, apart from Android. To check the Linux tab in headless Chrome, pass --user-agent= with a Linux user agent string. custom.css styles the tabs on a blue line, with the selected tab in lime.
  • Other content per operating system goes in {{< os-tabs >}}, with a {{< os-tab name="macOS" >}} and then a {{< os-tab name="Linux" >}} inside it, each holding Markdown, as Installing’s requirements tables do. It uses the same tabs, styles and script as the install commands, so the visitor’s system is selected, and the build fails unless the tabs are macOS’s, then Linux’s.
  • Colors: the site is dark only (hugo.yaml’s params.theme). Its palette is in docs/assets/css/custom.css: a black background and one lime accent, #7fff00, which sets Hextra’s primary color. The home page’s illustrations also use #0086b3, the blue that Hextra’s syntax highlighting gives commands like cd, and #ff5370 (--devvm-red), the JustBlack theme’s red, which marks only what an attack has compromised. The red’s contrast is 6.7:1 on the black and 6.0:1 on the surface color, and it’s much darker than the lime, so the two stay apart for readers who can’t tell red from green.
  • Fonts: the site uses Instrument Sans for text, Martian Mono for code, and Departure Mono, a pixel font, for the logo and the home page’s headings, badge and buttons. All three are in docs/static/fonts/, each in its own folder with its license, and docs/layouts/_partials/custom/head-end.html declares them. Instrument Sans and Martian Mono are upstream’s variable WOFF2 files, so one file holds every weight, and the partial’s comment records where each font came from, at which commit or release, and its SHA-256. To update a font, download the new version from the same place, check its SHA-256, and update the comment. Departure Mono is sharp at multiples of 11px and has one weight.
  • No third-party requests: devvm.dev and next.devvm.dev load every script, stylesheet, font and image from the site itself, so a visitor’s browser asks no other host for anything. mise run lint:docs checks this after it builds the site: TestNoThirdPartyLoads in internal/cli/docgen/site_test.go reads every page and stylesheet and fails on a link, script, image, frame or CSS url() that points at a host other than the ones in hugo.yaml’s and next.yaml’s baseURL. Hugo fetches FlexSearch, which Hextra’s search uses, when it builds the site, and the site serves it itself, so it passes. Diagrams are SVGs inside the pages, so they load nothing. Links that a visitor clicks, such as GitHub’s, aren’t loads, and the check ignores them. The social cards draw it from docs/assets/fonts/departure-mono/, which has the same release’s OTF and license, because Hugo can’t draw text from a WOFF2.
  • The logo in the navbar is the branding page’s devvm-logo-on-dark.svg at its own size, which hugo.yaml’s params.navbar.logo names, with the site’s title as its alt text. Right-clicking it opens the branding page instead of the browser’s menu, through a script in docs/layouts/_partials/custom/footer.html. A left click, or Enter on the focused logo, still goes to the home page.
  • The branding page is docs/content/branding.md, at /branding/, on its own layout, docs/layouts/branding.html, which is Hextra’s home layout with the home page’s look and the script that copies a swatch’s hex. Its front matter keeps it out of the sidebar. It has the logo as box-drawing text in a code block, the logo’s SVGs and PNGs, the icons, the social card, the palette, the fonts, how to use the logo and the credits.
    • Its downloads are in docs/static/branding/, and {{< brand-asset >}} tiles inside {{< brand-assets >}} show each one on its background, with a link to each file. The build fails when a file doesn’t exist, and it reads each PNG’s size for its link. devvm-logo-on-dark.svg and devvm-logo-on-light.svg are the logo, drawn on a pixel grid as the favicon is, made from Departure Mono’s 11px glyphs. The prompt and devvm are at twice the glyphs’ size, the box is in 1-pixel lines, and the lock, a block with a keyhole under a 2-pixel arch, sits on the box’s bottom-right corner, with the box’s lines stopping short of it so that the arch stands clear. The version for light backgrounds is black, with its prompt in the dark lime, #408000 (--devvm-accent-dark), which is the lime’s hue at half its lightness, with a contrast of 4.9:1 on white, where the lime has 1.2:1. Each logo’s PNG is its SVG at four times its size on a transparent background, and devvm-icon-64.png to devvm-icon-1024.png are docs/static/favicon.svg at 4 to 64 times its size. After changing an SVG, render its PNGs again with headless Chrome’s --screenshot at the exact size, passing --default-background-color=00000000 for the logos’ transparency, and look at each one.
    • The palette comes from {{< palette >}}, which reads the colors that docs/data/palette.yaml lists, with each one’s name and use, and takes each hex from its variable in custom.css, so the page always shows the site’s colors. The build fails when a variable isn’t there. A new color goes in both files.
    • The fonts each come from {{< font-sample >}}, which shows a line of text in the font, with a link to the license the site serves for it.
  • The favicon is the same mark drawn on a 16-pixel grid in docs/static/favicon.svg: the box, a lime prompt in its middle and a small lock centered on its bottom-right corner, overhanging it by 2 pixels each way, its shackle a closed arch, with the box’s lines stopping a pixel short of the lock, on black, with a pixel of black around the whole mark. Hextra links its icons by name, and the ones in docs/static/ take the place of its own: favicon-16x16.png and favicon-32x32.png, favicon.ico, which holds those two PNGs, apple-touch-icon.png, which is the grid at 160px with 10px of black around it, and the two android-chrome-*.png icons that site.webmanifest lists. Each PNG is the SVG at a whole multiple of its size, so its pixels stay sharp. The social card in docs/static/images/social-card.png is the 1200x630 card that the branding page offers for links to devvm. It has devvm-logo-on-dark.svg at twice its size, the home page’s headline and tagline in Departure Mono, and the site’s colors. After changing the SVG or the card’s text, render the PNGs again with headless Chrome’s --screenshot at the image’s exact size, and look at each one.
  • Social cards: every page gets a 1200x630 card of its own, which Hugo draws when it builds the site, and which sites and chat apps show when someone shares the page’s link.
    • The card is docs/assets/images/og-template.png, which is social-card.png with the headline and tagline painted out in the background’s black, so it has the logo, devvm.dev and the lime bar, in the same four colors and nothing else. docs/layouts/_partials/og-image.html draws three things on it with Hugo’s images.Text, in Departure Mono: the page’s section in lime capitals at 22px, its title in white at 66px, or at 55px or 44px when a smaller size fits it in two lines, and its explainer in gray at 33px. A docs page’s section is its section’s title, such as Using devvm, a section’s own page has Docs, and the home page and the branding page have none. The text is centered between the logo and devvm.dev. Each size is a multiple of 11px and each line starts at a whole pixel, so the text is as sharp as the logo, and the card keeps only the template’s four colors. docs/layouts/_partials/og-wrap.html wraps the lines at spaces, and because the font is monospaced, a line’s width is its length.
    • The explainer is the explainer in each page’s front matter: a few plain words on what the reader gets from the page, such as Install devvm and check what it needs, without a full stop. It isn’t the page’s description, which search engines and llms.txt show, because that’s a sentence or two, and most pages have none. The home page’s card shows its cardTitle, the hero’s headline, in place of its title, because the logo already says devvm. The CLI reference’s pages get their command’s Short as their explainer when mise run cli-docs writes them. TestExplainers in internal/cli/docgen fails when a page has no explainer, or when its explainer takes more than two lines of 48 characters or its title more than two lines of 36, which are the card’s lines at 33px and 44px.
    • The tags: docs/layouts/_partials/custom/head-end.html writes og:image with its type, width, height and og:image:alt, and twitter:image:alt, whose text is devvm docs, the title and the explainer. docs/layouts/_partials/_funcs/get-page-images.html takes the place of Hugo’s own, which its Twitter card and schema templates call for a page’s images, so twitter:image and the schema’s image are the same card. hugo.yaml names no params.images, so Hextra’s Open Graph template writes no second og:image. A card’s address is the site’s, so next.devvm.dev’s pages show next.devvm.dev’s cards.
  • The illustrations on the home page are SVGs in docs/assets/home/, and {{< art "name" >}} inlines one into the page, so that it gets the page’s fonts and colors. A feature card’s art parameter inlines one the same way, through docs/layouts/_partials/art.html. Each one is drawn on Departure Mono’s 11px cell, 7 pixels wide and 14 tall, so its text and shapes are sharpest at its own size or at twice its size. The art shortcode shows it at twice its size, 728px wide. A card shows it as wide as the card, at whatever scale that takes.
    • Each card’s drawing shows what its text says, and nothing more. The big cards’ drawings are 364 by 140 pixels, or 168 for isolated.svg: zero-config.svg shows a dev server’s forwarded port, devvm code and a commit authored by you, copies.svg the base image and its copies, isolated.svg the mount and the proxy, agents.svg the agents’ mounts, the history that stays and the token, and make-it-yours.svg the stack of base, your layer and the VM, with --from. The What’s supported cards’ drawings are 224 by 70 pixels: toolchains.svg, coding-agents.svg and layers.svg, which shows the image docker+nix as a stack and the built-in layers beside it. The Quick start cards’ drawings are terminals of 254 by 181 pixels, which a card shows at most twice their size: step-cd.svg types cd ~/some-project on your machine, step-pick.svg types devvm, shows a short version of the new VM’s summary and presses enter at Customize it? [y/N], and step-agent.svg types claude in the VM’s shell. Why use devvm?’s drawing, blast-radius.svg, is 364 by 210 pixels and shows the same four attacks as its text on two machines. Without devvm, they light up on your machine, and the project, ~/.aws, ~/.ssh and another project turn red one after another. With devvm, they light up in the VM, each one’s path toward your machine ends at the VM’s border with a cross, and your machine’s folders stay as they are.
    • Every text element holds one run of characters at its own x, because Hugo’s --minify removes the spaces between tspan elements. A gap of a cell is 7 pixels added to x.
    • Animations are CSS keyframes in custom.css, which classes in the SVGs turn on. pulse dims and brightens a lime arrow every 3 seconds, and pulse-2 and pulse-3 start a part of the arrow 0.3 and 0.6 seconds later, so the pulse runs along it. pulse-slow does the same every 4 seconds. lit lights a text’s fill and lit-chip a chip’s opacity for most of a 4-second loop, and lit-2, lit-3 and lit-4 start them 0.5, 1 and 1.5 seconds later, so they light one after another. blink turns a cursor on and off every 2 seconds. mover marks a block that travels a path, mover-token along the token’s line, under the proxy and down to the API in 3 seconds, and mover-egress under the proxy, down to the allowlist and back, then out to the internet in 4 seconds. A block is drawn before the shapes it passes under. attack-1 to attack-4, path-1 to path-4 and reach-1 to reach-4 tell blast-radius.svg’s story in an 8-second loop, and every part of the drawing stays in place all along, so the story only changes colours and draws lines. Each attack’s chip turns from gray to lime at 0.4, 1.6, 2.8 and 4 seconds. In the VM, its path then draws itself down to the VM’s border, and when it gets there, the cross at the border turns lime and, on the machine without devvm, the folder it reaches turns red. Everything holds from 5.2 seconds, and from 6.6 seconds the colours go back and the paths draw back up, so the drawing rests from 7.2 seconds until the story starts again. Each step has its own keyframes, so that all of them end together. The SVG draws each part in its end colour, and --rest in custom.css gives the colour it has before its step, so a drawing without animation shows the end of the story. The Quick start terminals each loop on their own. type marks a cover over a command, which shrinks from the right one cell at a time while caret moves the cursor along, both in --chars steps across --width, and caret-blink keeps the cursor solid while it types and makes it blink after. In step-pick.svg, pick-summary shows the summary once devvm is typed, pick-ask shows the question after it, and key lights enter as it’s pressed. Their styles in custom.css are each part’s end state too, and their keyframes start from the beginning. When the visitor’s system asks for reduced motion, prefers-reduced-motion turns every animation off and hides the blocks.
    • To see an animation’s state in a screenshot, pause the animations with a stylesheet of your own and set each class’s animation-delay to minus the time you want, because headless Chrome’s --virtual-time-budget barely moves CSS animations.
  • Icons are pixel icons in docs/assets/icons/, one SVG per icon. Most come from Dinkie Icons, which is MIT licensed, and the folder keeps its license and a README that names the version they were copied from. The penguin, prompt, warning and light bulb icons are drawn for devvm in the same style. {{< icon "rocket" >}} inlines one through docs/layouts/_partials/icon.html, so it takes the text’s color, and the build fails when no icon has that name. An icon is 0.75em square, which makes each of its pixels one screen pixel in 16px text, and it sits on the text’s baseline. Screen readers skip it, unless a second argument gives it a label, as in {{< icon "warning" "Warning" >}}, for an icon that says something the text doesn’t. To add a Dinkie icon, copy its path data from the same version of the @dinkie-icons/react npm package into a new file named after the icon in kebab case, with the same svg attributes as the others. A new icon of your own uses the same 12-pixel grid and 1-pixel lines, and the README lists it.
    • Each section’s icon is chosen once, in docs/data/sections.yaml, which maps a section’s folder under docs/ to an icon’s name, as in getting-started: rocket. A new section gets a line there. The section cards and the sidebar both read it, so they always show the same icon, and the build fails when the list names a section or an icon that doesn’t exist.
    • Section cards on the docs’ first page are Hextra’s {{< cards >}} holding a {{< section-card path="getting-started" >}} for each section, with its one-line description inside, closed with {{< /section-card >}}. The shortcode takes the section’s title and link from its page under docs/, and its icon from sections.yaml, and the build fails when there’s no such page. Hextra’s card takes an icon only from Hextra’s own set, so the shortcode puts ours in the card’s title, at 24px. It’s dimmed as Hextra dims its own cards’ icons, and it turns lime on hover.
    • The sidebar’s top-level items show their section’s icon at 12px, in the link’s color, so it’s gray, and lime for the section you’re in. Hextra’s sidebar has no icons, so docs/layouts/_partials/custom/head-end.html writes a CSS rule for each section when the site builds, keyed to the section page’s address, with the icon from docs/assets/icons/ as a mask. Nothing is generated into the repo, so there’s no step to rerun.
    • The OS tabs of install and os-tabs show the Apple icon before macOS and the penguin before Linux, which docs/layouts/_partials/os-tab-name.html adds to each tab’s name.
    • ✓ and ✗ go before a table cell’s word: {{< yes >}} yes puts a lime check before it, and {{< no >}} doesn't a gray cross. They go only in cells that are a plain yes or no, or what stands for one, such as the install script’s offers it, never in cells that are sentences, and the word stays, because screen readers skip the icon. Icons in tables are 12px, because a table’s text is smaller than 16px.
    • Buttons take an icon before their text: docs/layouts/_shortcodes/hextra/hero-button.html is Hextra’s hero-button with an icon parameter, as in {{< hextra/hero-button text="Install" link="docs/getting-started/install/" icon="download" >}}, drawn at 24px like the headings’ icons. The 404 page’s two buttons have their icons in its layout, a rocket for Getting started and the open book for the docs, as the home page’s Read the docs has it.
    • The navbar’s GitHub link uses Dinkie’s GitHub icon, which docs/data/icons.yaml adds to Hextra’s own icons as dinkie-github, and hugo.yaml’s menu names. Hextra’s icon partial reads only that data, so an icon for the navbar goes there as its SVG, not in docs/assets/icons/.
  • Heading icons: a heading gets an icon before its text with an icon attribute, as in ## Quick start {icon="rocket"}, which the home page’s section headings use. docs/layouts/_markup/render-heading.html takes the place of Hextra’s heading render hook and adds the icon after Hugo makes the heading’s anchor, so the anchor comes from the text alone, such as quick-start. On the home page, custom.css draws these icons in lime at 24px, so each icon pixel is two screen pixels, as each of Departure Mono’s pixels is at 22px.
  • Callouts are GitHub’s alerts: a blockquote whose first line is [!NOTE], [!TIP] or [!WARNING], which GitHub shows the same way. docs/layouts/_markup/render-blockquote-alert.html takes the place of Hextra’s alerts and draws each one on the surface color with a line down its left side, and a title with its icon: information-circled in blue for a note, the light bulb in the soft lime for a tip, and warning in lime for a warning. Any other type fails the build. Hextra’s own callout shortcode isn’t used. Use a callout only for a real warning, such as what the VM’s boundary rests on, or a tip that saves the reader trouble, such as keeping a VM on a strict tier, and move the sentence into it instead of repeating it.
  • For agents and other tools that read the site, hugo.yaml turns on three things that Hextra has. The site’s root has llms.txt, which lists every section and its pages. Each page has a Markdown copy beside its HTML, such as /docs/using/clone.md beside /docs/using/clone/, and a section’s copy is index.md in its folder, such as /docs/using/index.md. Each docs page has a Copy page menu beside its title, which copies the page’s Markdown or opens it. hugo.yaml lists every output for the home page, the sections and the pages, so the home page and the sections keep their RSS feeds, and the search index is built apart from these outputs.
    • llms.txt comes from docs/layouts/llms.txt, which takes the place of Hextra’s. It has the site’s title and description, then each section under its title, with the section’s own page first and its pages after it. Each one is a link to its Markdown copy, as the llms.txt convention prefers, which docs/layouts/_partials/llms-link.txt writes, and a line of plain text, which docs/layouts/_partials/llms-summary.txt writes. A page without a copy gets a link to its HTML page instead. The line is the page’s description from its front matter when it has one, and otherwise its first paragraph, cut at 200 characters. A description is also the page’s description for search engines and link previews, so give a page one when its first paragraph doesn’t say what the page covers, as Coding agents has. llms.txt also lists the CLI reference, with each command’s one-line summary.
    • The Markdown copies come from docs/layouts/page.markdown.md and section.markdown.md, which take the place of Hextra’s and both use docs/layouts/_partials/markdown-copy.md. A copy is the page’s title as a heading, then its Markdown with its shortcodes rendered. In a copy, a link to a section’s _index.md points at index.md, the section copy’s name, so the links work between the copies, and a link written in code stays as it is.
    • Each shortcode that docs pages use has a Markdown version beside its HTML one in docs/layouts/_shortcodes/, named after it with .markdown.md, which renders it in the copies. install writes each system’s name in bold, then its commands, which come from docs/layouts/_partials/install-tabs.html, the same partial its tabs use. os-tabs writes its tabs the same way, through docs/layouts/_partials/os-sections.md. section-card makes a list item that links the section’s copy, and Hextra’s cards keeps only what’s inside it. yes and no become ✓ and ✗. A shortcode without a Markdown version puts its HTML into the copy.
    • The home page and the branding page are mostly shortcodes, and neither layout shows the menu. hugo.yaml gives the home page no Markdown copy, and its front matter sets contextMenu: false. The branding page’s front matter sets outputs: [html], contextMenu: false and llms: false, so it has no copy, no menu and no line in llms.txt. Any other page can set llms: false to stay out of llms.txt, or contextMenu: false to have no menu.
    • After you add a page or a shortcode, build the site and read the page’s line in llms.txt and its Markdown copy. The line should say what the page covers, and the copy should have no shortcode left in it, such as {{< os-tabs >}}, and no HTML from one. A shortcode that docs pages use gets its Markdown version. To try the menu, serve the site with mise run docs and open a docs page. custom.css gives the menu the site’s border and secondary text, lime on hover, and its list the surface color.
  • The 404 page is docs/layouts/404.html, which takes the place of Hextra’s and uses the site’s navbar and footer. It shows a VM’s terminal answering cd ./this-page with “no such page”, drawn like the home page’s art in docs/assets/home/not-found.svg with the blink cursor, then Hextra’s search box and links to Getting started and the docs. Build the site and open /404.html to see it.

mise run lint:docs, which mise run lint includes, checks docs/ with:

Linter Checks Config
markdownlint-cli2 Markdown .markdownlint-cli2.yaml
Vale the style rules .vale.ini, .vale/styles/devvm/
lychee (--offline) links to pages and files

It also builds the site with Hugo’s --panicOnWarning, into a temporary folder it removes, so any warning fails it. That includes a deprecation, such as a template that reads site.Data where Hugo wants hugo.Data, so a Hugo upgrade that deprecates something the templates use fails here before the feature is removed. It runs TestExplainers too, so a page without an explainer fails it, and TestUserPageProse (internal/cli/docgen/prose_test.go), which holds the user pages to lead with doing: it fails a run of three or more paragraphs back to back where two are over 80 words, and any paragraph or list item over 150 words. It counts words as scan.sh does, a code span as one word and a link by its text, and a paragraph of 40 words or fewer that ends with a colon introduces what follows, so it isn’t in a run. proseExempt names the pages that another branch is rewriting, each with why, until that branch lands. TestChangelogShape (internal/cli/docgen/changelog_test.go) holds CHANGELOG.md to the shape that Releasing gives an entry, and TestChangelogProblems checks that each of its rules fails an entry that breaks it.

The CLI reference

The CLI reference in docs/content/docs/cli/ is generated from devvm’s commands with Cobra’s docs generator, and checked in. Don’t edit it: change the command’s Use, Short, Long, Example or flags, or its docs page in internal/msg/docs.go, then run:

mise run cli-docs

It runs internal/cli/docgen, which replaces every page in that folder: _index.md, listing the commands, and a page per command named after its path (devvm_build.md), with title and explainer front matter, the explainer being the command’s Short, and links to the other pages as files. Each page has the command’s examples, and a Docs section before See also that links to the command’s docs page on the site. Hidden commands (_msg, _qemu) and Cobra’s help command are left out. The pages carry no dates, so the same commands give the same files. They carry no weight either, so Hugo sorts the section by title, and a new command adds its own page and changes only _index.md and the root’s devvm.md; TestPagesHaveNoWeight checks this. The .gitattributes file marks the pages as generated, so GitHub collapses them in a diff.

mise run cli-docs also writes the generated blocks of hand-written pages, which cli.DocBlocks in internal/cli/docblocks.go lists: the Supported agents table in using/coding-agents.md, and the README’s list of the agents. Each block sits between two HTML comments that name it, and docgen replaces only the text between them, from the registry of agents, agents.Defs, and each agent’s policy in assets/shared-tools/. So don’t edit a block by hand: change the agent’s Def, its Docs included, or its policy, then run mise run cli-docs.

A command’s help

Every command’s help, which its reference page also shows, has the same shape. Short is an action in sentence case without a full stop, such as List the project VMs. Long is one to three short sentences on what the command does, and the rules and edge cases go on its docs page. Example comes from examples in internal/cli/help.go, which takes each command line with a short comment and lines the comments up, the most common invocation first. A flag’s description is short, and its long explanation goes on the page.

Each command describes itself where it’s made, so its docs page and group are in its own file, not in tables elsewhere. Its Annotations come from an about in internal/cli/help.go: docs, the user page that covers it as page#anchor; group, its section of the root’s help; and noJSON, why a command without --json has none. addDocs gives the root Cobra’s usage template with a Docs section at the end, which shows the address of the command’s page, and the root’s help also ends with the issue tracker, msg.IssuesURL. The CLI reference links each command’s page too, and TestDocLinks in internal/msg reads those links from the reference and checks that each page and heading exists and is a user page. helpGroups in the same file lists the root’s sections, in order, and addGroups adds each group that has a command and sets its commands’ GroupID, so a group whose commands don’t exist yet stays out of the help. A subcommand can name a group too, such as layer add in Change your VM, when it belongs in another group than its parent. addGroups then adds that group to the parent, so the parent’s own help groups its subcommands the same way, and the usage template lists the subcommand by both names in the root’s group, after the group’s own commands. Cobra lists a group’s commands in alphabetical order, and help goes in Cobra’s own Additional Commands.

The tests fail when the checked-in pages are stale: TestReferenceIsCurrent in internal/cli/docgen generates the reference into a temporary folder and compares it with docs/content/docs/cli/, and it checks each generated block against its page too, which TestStaleBlockIsCaught proves it catches. mise run docs regenerates it before serving the site.

Building the site

mise run docs draws the diagrams, then serves the site at http://localhost:1313/ and reloads on every change except a diagram’s, which needs mise run docs:diagrams again. After you run mise run docs:diagrams, mise exec -- hugo -s docs --minify builds the site into docs/public/, as the Docs workflow does for devvm.dev, and mise exec -- hugo -s docs --minify --config hugo.yaml,next.yaml builds the site as next.devvm.dev has it, with its banner and its noindex (the docs sites).

item.title: Design notes
item.description:
